lines.2017年7月，從蒙古共和國首都烏蘭巴托，飛往蘇聯西伯利亞最大城市 Irkuts: In July 2017, from Ulaanbaatar, capital of the Republic of Mongolia, I flew to Irkutsk, the largest city in Soviet Siberia, then took a car to the small lakeside town of Listvyanka on Lake Baikal. At dawn I walked along the lake, watching white mist and hazy groves of trees, the rising sun floating on the clear lake surface, half-veiling the distant mountain ridges. The next day, heading north, I took a ferry to Olkhon Island, the largest island on Lake Baikal, and stayed two nights, admiring the scenery and waters along the island's shores.

lines.Cesky Krumlov 和Karlovy Vary 是捷克波西米亞平原上的主: Cesky Krumlov and Karlovy Vary are the main tourist destinations on the Bohemian plain of the Czech Republic. Cesky Krumlov (a shallow shoal in a river bend) sits in a deep valley through which the Vltava River winds, a fairy-tale-like beautiful small town. Since the 14th century, developed under the Rosenberg family and the Habsburg dynasty, its castle architecture is grounded in the Renaissance style, layered with Baroque and Rococo flourishes, making the riverside town, though miniature, exquisite -- classical yet elegant. The castle, the square, the narrow lanes are all touched with soft, lovely colors, exuding a quiet, nostalgic atmosphere. It is a poetic small town steeped in history yet forgotten by time; walking its simple, unassuming streets and alleys feels like lingering inside a story, a dream. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1992.

lines.Karlovy Vary 位於捷克西部，距布拉格約二個小時車程。坐落於溫泉水源地: Karlovy Vary lies in the western Czech Republic, about a two-hour drive from Prague. Situated in a region of hot spring waters, it is a famous spa town. Within the city there are 13 major hot springs and more than three hundred smaller ones; visitors may drink the freely flowing spring water at any time. Spa cup, plus spa wafer, plus spa liqueur, equals a spa town. In German the city is called Karlsbad, named for the Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, Charles IV, who founded the city in 1370. The "bad" in Karlsbad is the German root for hot spring. It has long been a resort for royalty and nobility, and many writers and musicians -- Goethe, Schiller, Beethoven, Mozart, Schumann, Tchaikovsky, and others -- left their footsteps here. On the town's outskirts is a small park with their statues. In the town there is also a statue garden for the Czech composer Antonin Dvorak, radiating the rich melodic beauty of his "New World Symphony." Though Karlovy Vary is likewise threaded by a river, its scenery and style differ from the fairy-tale Cesky Krumlov -- its townscape is orderly, its colors resplendent and elegant, mature and dignified, classical yet fashionable, and it is also home to one of the world's five major film festivals.

lines.《沉思者》是羅丹《地獄門》上的重要作品之一，原名《 詩人》。關於作品中人物身分的: "The Thinker" is one of the important works on Rodin's "The Gates of Hell," originally titled "The Poet." Regarding the identity of the figure in the work, two views currently exist. One school holds that this thinker represents the image of the poet Dante. The other, based on Rodin's own statements and on the nude rendering of the figure, holds that "The Thinker" is the embodiment of all "poets" and "creators," pondering how to achieve liberation of the soul through poetic and artistic creation. Whichever view one takes, Rodin omits detail in the facial features, yet through his emphasis on light, shadow, and the modeling of musculature, brilliantly conveys the complex inner thoughts of the thinker. The taut muscles, the deep-cut lines, the restrained yet tension-filled body seem to bear the heavy entanglements of your life and mine, agonizing over the unsolvable puzzles of humankind.

In this dazzling metropolis, Mondrian felt a world free of the turmoil of war, pulsing with the fresh spirit of the modern city. Broadway Boogie Woogie is a major work from Mondrian's New York period, and also the last piece he completed before his death. It is still made of straight lines, but not the cold, austere black boundary lines — instead, lively, dancing lines of color, composed of small rectangles of varying colors and lengths, lightly dividing the picture plane. It is still primary colors, but no longer bound by black lines; instead bright yellow predominates, interspersed with red and blue, forming vivid colored lines, among which are scattered blocks of red, yellow, and blue, creating the rhythmic shifts and vibrating frequencies of jazz.

lines.從台東縣鹿野，關山，池上，到花蓮縣富里，玉里，壽豐，綿延近百里的這段地區，是花東: From Luye, Guanshan, and Chishang in Taitung County, to Fuli, Yuli, and Shoufeng in Hualien County, this stretch of nearly a hundred miles is the rice-growing region of the East Rift Valley. Because the water and soil are pure and unpolluted, it yields glistening, translucent white rice that, once cooked, is soft and pleasantly sticky, with a faint fragrance — its quality unmatched anywhere in Taiwan. Across this lush green expanse of paddies, during the winter fallow season from December through January and February, farmers plant canola in the fields as organic green fertilizer. So from mid-January on, the vast blooming sea of canola flowers becomes one of the East Rift Valley's most enchanting sights. Each small yellow flower is unremarkable alone, but when the canola fields stretch field after field to the horizon, they form a magnificent expanse of golden brilliance, set against blue sky and white clouds, green mountains and clear water — a pastoral scene of transcendent beauty that has become the East Rift Valley's signature landscape. To make the valley's winter scenery even more vibrant, in recent years some farmers have begun planting the vividly colored cosmos as well, creating a more varied sea of flowers to draw an even livelier tide of visitors.

To the left, Yushan cane spreads in a sweep, draping the slopes in a dazzling carpet of orange-yellow. Scattered Taiwan firs stand tenaciously above it. Nanhu Mountain and Zhongyangjian Mountain gaze at each other across the northern sky. Farther still must be Siyuan Pass, worn away over a thousand years by the Dajia and Lanyang Rivers! To the right, the cliffs of Hehuan Mountain rise in layered, folded rock, their texture like a painting, clusters of snow clinging to the sheer walls and dripping into thin trickling streams. Qilai Mountain and Nenggao Mountain stretch along the southeastern horizon, forming ridges and ranges amid drifting mist and cloud.

lines.旅遊埃及時，觀賞了許多神廟古殿遺跡，体驗古埃及宏偉精巧的文明形態和內涵。參觀 A: While traveling in Egypt, I viewed many ancient temples and palace ruins, experiencing the grand and intricate form and substance of ancient Egyptian civilization. When visiting the Kom Ombo Temple near Aswan, it happened to be dusk, and the glow of the setting sun scattered across the broken pillars and ruined walls, casting off a soft, desolate afterglow like the last gleam before darkness. I saw an old man sitting withered before the temple, his expression distant, faintly evoking the ancient-and-modern contrast of 'a thousand years of glory left behind, ten years of life returning to solitude.' Lingering there, reluctant to leave, I could not help but recall, beyond time and space, Deshan Temple near Zhushan in Nantou.

lines.波西米亞 (捷克語，Cechy ; 拉丁語，Bohemia ) 有地理，歷史和: Bohemia (Czech: Čechy; Latin: Bohemia) carries geographic, historical, and cultural meaning. Historically, the Kingdom of Bohemia was an ancient Central European state, once a kingdom within the Holy Roman Empire, later becoming a province of the Austrian Habsburg monarchy. Between 1919 and 1992 it was, intermittently, part of Czechoslovakia, and after 1993 it became the core of the Czech Republic. Culturally, Bohemia refers to the Bohemian style — an artistic temperament, a refined, faintly decadent elegance, an anti-traditional, free-spirited, romantic way of life and fashion. In the 19th century the French writer Henri Murger wrote a novel, Scenes of Bohemian Life, from which the name and meaning of Bohemian arose. The Italian opera composer Puccini, based on that novel, created the classic opera La Bohème (also translated as The Life of an Artist, 1896). Geographically, Bohemia lies in the Bohemian Plain at the heart of the European continent, comprising mainly the broad lands of west-central Czechia (including the capital, Prague) along with small adjoining parts of Germany, Poland, and Austria. It has a landscape of sweeping, rolling hills and forests, and a varied, vibrant human character. It is a gathering place of the wandering Roma people. Within its borders runs the Czech Republic's longest river, the Vltava, which flows from the southwest through Český Krumlov, north through Prague, under the Charles Bridge, and onward north into the Elbe.

Today, the less-than-ten-thousand-hectare pure stand of cypress on Mount Qilan and the red cypress forest along the Xiuguluan River are, remarkably, the world's two last surviving great cypress forests. These two natural treasures, left by the heavens to Taiwan and to all humankind, are still eyed covetously by forestry officials and business interests, endangered by a mindset in government and academia that favors profit over the forests, and by the raids of illegal loggers -- the cypress forests are being lost bit by bit. Taiwan's great forest catastrophe of the twentieth century, and whether these two surviving cypress forests can endure into the future, is a grave test facing twenty-first century Taiwan -- a test of the Taiwanese people's land ethic, their feeling for mountain forests, and their sense of Taiwanese identity.

lines.這幅畫可以說是克林姆繪畫生涯的最高峰。畫中裹在金色衣飾裡的男子和女子，在花朵盛開: This painting may be called the pinnacle of Klimt's career. A man and woman, wrapped in golden robes, embrace tightly at the edge of a blossoming cliff. One can almost feel the intensity of the man's kiss. The woman's expression is alluring, her eyes shut tight, her right hand clenched into a fist—it is unclear whether she resists or yields. Klimt's fame as a painter comes not only from his use of real gold, but from how, in this series, he fused the abstract and the realistic to perfection. The figures' forms are true to life, while the ornamentation of their garments dissolves into illusory geometric patterns. (Austrian Gallery, Belvedere, Vienna)

lines.雖說冬天是蕭索的，在婆娑之洋，美麗之島，卻也有一番金黄溫潤的景色。不管是豐收還是: Although winter is said to be bleak, on this ocean of swaying waves, this beautiful island, there is nonetheless a scene of golden, mellow warmth. Whether the harvest is bountiful or lean, once the second rice crop is reaped, the turned-over soil reveals field after field of differing rural scenery. Many farmers scatter canola seed across the freshly turned earth. Undeterred by the cold wind and chilling rain, by frozen ground and silent soil, the seeds sprout on their own, grow, bud, and then burst into countless small yellow blossoms, unfurling into acre upon acre of golden canola fields. notes.Taj Mahal (泰姬瑪哈陵)，這座鑲嵌了28種寶石的白色大理石陵墓，是蒙兀: Taj Mahal (Taj Mahal), a white marble mausoleum set with 28 stones, was built by Shah Jahan, the fifth emperor of the Mughal dynasty (Genghis Khan's descendants entered northern India from Central Asia and established the Mughal Empire, 1526-1758) in memory of his beloved queen. Construction began in 1631 and involved 20,000 artisans from India and Central Asia over a period of 22 years. The planning and design of the mausoleum is a combination of Persian, Central Asian Islamic architecture and traditional Hindu architecture, which not only has magnificent beauty and geometric shape, but also exudes harmony, serenity and a solemn poetic atmosphere. Marble buildings change color subtly with the light of the clouds.
notes.16世紀有三個穆斯林帝國擁有遼濶的地盤，其中之—就是位於印度的蒙兀兒王朝， 其首: In the 16th century, there were three Muslim empires with Liaoning territory, one of which was the Mughal dynasty in India, and its capital was Angra. Today, Angola is an authentic northern Indian city, but with three World Heritage Sites: Taj Mahal, Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri, it is India's most popular tourist city. Agra Fort is a masterpiece of Hindu-Islamic art at its peak, a fortified castle and a majestic palace. It is a magnificent structure built by Akbar the Great of the Mughal Empire over a period of 8 years, and continued to expand until the reign of his grandson Shah Jahan. However, at the height of his prosperity, Shah Jahan was confined to the castle by his own son. The 20-meter red sandstone rock wall built by his grandfather at that time became a prison wall that was difficult to overcome. He could only sit in the small building in the city and look at him — the white Taj Mahal built by his hand, and miss his wife.
notes.Orchha (歐恰古城) 始建於16世紀，曾經是拉傑普特人Rajput所建立的: Founded in the 16th century, Orchha was once the capital of the Kingdom of Bandera, founded by the Rajputs, and is now a remote and small village. Hundreds of years later, — a prosperous capital city decayed into a small village, not surprisingly, despite the countless wars and man-made disasters, the walls, palaces and temples of that year were fully preserved. Although there are such magnificent and exquisite ancient buildings, there are few tourists — quiet. Walk into the castle and walk through palaces and temples, filled with mulberry murals and sculptures. Overlooking the city from afar, the ancient buildings scattered in the woods are looming, and even the small towns nestled in the mountains and rivers are drenched in antiquity and coolness.
notes.Khajuraho小鎮在10到13世紀是昌德拉王朝的首都，其極盛時期是在公元10: The town of Khajuraho was the capital of the Chandra dynasty from the 10th to the 13th centuries, and its peak was around 1000 AD, when most of the Cagiuraho temples seen today were built. Historically, various clansmen have listed sex as taboo, and today's India is also quite conservative in terms of male and female love. However, this group of Indian temples built a thousand years ago, almost every temple wall is carved with pictures of sex between men and women, and its boldness is bold enough to make modern people tongue-tied. The beliefs of the clan, the concept of human nature, the norms of life, the sculpture skills and the artistic viewpoint contained in the wall sculpture are all impressive and revealing.
notes.Varanasi (瓦拉納西) 位於恆河岸邊的中等城市，卻保留著1500多座寺廟: Located in a medium-sized city on the banks of the Ganges River, Varanasi has more than 1,500 temples and more than 400 festivals every year. The Buddha Shakyamuni preached here in the 5th century BC, and the high priest Xuanzheng of the Tang Dynasty in China came here in the 7th century AD to worship and learn the Sutras. Tenth-century Muslims occupied the area until the eighteenth century, during which many mosques were built. Still, Varanasi was famous for its Hinduism. Drinking Ganges water, paying homage to Shiva, making friends with saints, and living in Varanasi are the greatest wishes of the Hindus in their lifetime. More than 80% of Indians are Hindustani, and Varanasi is the territory of Shiva, the holy place of Hindustani.
notes.恆河 (Gange River) 發源於喜馬拉雅山的冰川，長2500公里，流經印: The Gange River originates from the glaciers of the Himalayas and flows 2,500 kilometers through the northeast of India and into the Bay of Bengal to the south. The four ancient civilizations of mankind are all river civilizations, but there is no river basin like the Ganges River Basin, which still retains the original myths and legends, rituals, ancient customs and lifestyles. notes.威尼斯嘉年華會 （ Carnival of Venice，義大利文為Carnev:
Carnival of Venice (Carnevale in Italian), also known as the Mask Festival, refers to the carnival before the fast. Its history can be traced back to the 11th century, when the Republic of Venice defeated the neighboring country of Ulrico, and people poured into the city of San Marco to celebrate their victory. After that, Venice became more and more powerful. After the 13th century, the carnival, which had been circulating for a long time, fixed the time according to the religious calendar, and it was held before the Easter Lent (Quaresima) every year for about 10-12 days under the name of "carnival". What is Lent? According to the Catholic calendar, Easter is held in March and April every year. In order to commemorate Jesus' crucifixion, the first 40 days of Easter were set as a fasting period, also known as "Lent". During this period, it is strictly forbidden for Christians to eat and drink for fun, so Christians are in a hurry to indulge themselves for a few days before fasting and enjoy themselves. (According to the source of the word carnevale for carnival, carnem (meat) + levale (remove, remove) in Latin, levare carne... the meaning of removing meat and not eating meat.)
The appearance of the mask (Masquerade) was around the 13th century. Because Venice was very prosperous, but it also widened the gap between the rich and poor between the nobility and the commoners, so during the carnival, everyone wore masks, dressed in the best costumes, and enjoyed the joy of the celebration together, regardless of class. Since it is a mask festival, that is, a masquerade party where you can dress up as you please, whether it is locals or tourists, at this time, you can leave reality behind, wear medieval costumes, with gorgeous jewelry and feathers, each one can become a dazzling protagonist in the court, and wear a sly and dramatic mask, which is not only mysterious but also full of imagination. (Compiled from Skyscanner, 2019)

The Little Penguin is, among the eighteen penguin species currently known, the smallest in size. It stands about 33 centimeters tall and weighs approximately 1 kilogram. Because of its small size it is also called the Fairy Penguin, and because its body is covered in deep blue feathers it is also called the Blue Penguin. The Maori of New Zealand call it "Korora." The Little Penguin is found mainly along the southern coast of Australia and the coasts of the North Island and northern South Island of New Zealand. Its total population is roughly one million, with Phillip Island south of Melbourne, Australia being its largest colony.
The Little Penguin is a hardworking wild bird. Like humans, it rises at dawn to work and rests at sunset, keeping house and raising its young with great toil. In fact, Little Penguins put out to sea before dawn, fishing, catching shrimp, and chasing squid and other prey in the wide, deep waters six nautical miles offshore, all while staying alert to avoid predators such as seals, sea lions, and skua gulls. Only at dusk do they swim back to shore, trudging home on tired, wobbling steps to feed their young. Although Little Penguins build their burrows near the coast, after coming ashore they still must walk some distance to reach home; people call their evening procession back to the nest the "Penguin Parade." Phillip Island Nature Park is a renowned spot for viewing Little Penguins — in the evening, visitors can sit on open-air viewing platforms on the beach and watch the penguins emerge one by one from the sea, wait for one another, then follow each other in single file across the beach and through the grass back home.

Among the three most treasured masterpieces of the Louvre Museum in Paris are the Mona Lisa, the statue of the Venus de Milo, and the Winged Victory of Samothrace. In the Mona Lisa, the supreme masterpiece by the Renaissance genius Leonardo da Vinci, Mona Lisa's mysterious hint of a smile has for centuries remained a riddle difficult to solve. It becomes a mystery because when a viewer looks closely and intently, the smile seems to vanish, leaving only a hazy, elusive expression that seems both present and absent. Precisely because of this "ungraspable smile," it has become known as the "mysterious smile."

notes.布萊德湖 ( Lake Bled ) 位於斯洛文尼亞 (Slovenia ) 的: Lake Bled is located in the northern part of Slovenia, within a branch range of the Alps, 55 kilometers from the capital Ljubljana. Lake Bled is a glacial lake, formed from meltwater from glaciers together with snowmelt flowing down from the Alps. Its waters are clear and cold, blue as silk, earning it the reputation of the "Ice Lake." The lake is 2.1 kilometers long and 1.4 kilometers wide, surrounded on all sides by snow-capped peaks and lush green forests, presenting a scene of serene and elegant beauty. An ancient castle stands on the lakeshore, and a white church on the island in the lake occasionally sends the sound of bells ringing out — nature and human culture reflecting and completing each other.
notes.布萊斯峽谷國家公園 (Bryce Canyon National Park) 位: Bryce Canyon National Park is located in southwestern Utah. About sixty million years ago, the Bryce Canyon area was a lake, and over the following millions of years, layers of limestone formed from mud and calcium carbonate accumulated one upon another. Geological movement 16 million years ago lifted the ancient lakebed to an elevation above 2,440 meters. Unlike the Grand Canyon, Bryce Canyon was not carved and eroded directly by a central river; rather, it was shaped by headward erosion from the Paria River, a tributary of the Colorado River, causing the cliffs to collapse. The harder limestone remained standing, and through centuries of rain, wind erosion, and the fine chiseling of ice, snow, and frost, it formed today's brilliantly colored and delicately carved rock spires (hoodoos), pinnacles, grottoes, and rock-wall "cathedrals," as well as the magnificent open-air amphitheater stretching more than 20 kilometers, unfurling like a long scroll suddenly opened before the viewer. Bryce Canyon has been likened to a natural hall of stone idols. In the 19th century, the Mormon settler Ebenezer Bryce cleared and farmed land here, and the area came to be called Bryce Canyon. It was designated a national park in 1928.

Poseidon, god of the sea, and Athena, goddess of wisdom, both wished to become the city's patron deity. So the gods decided to hold a "contest" to see whose gift to humankind would be more valuable. Poseidon struck the ground with his trident, and forth gushed seawater and a winged horse, symbolizing strength and mastery of the sea. Athena, in turn, offered an olive tree, symbolizing peace, wisdom, and a sustainable life. After deliberation, the gods concluded that the olive tree, which could provide food, oil, and timber, would bring the city lasting prosperity more surely than the power of war. And so the goddess Athena won! The city was thus named Athens, after her.

Geometry is a branch of mathematics that studies the shape, size, and positional relationships of objects.
Geometry has very early origins, traceable to ancient times. According to the ancient Greek historian Herodotus (c. 484–424 BC), because the periodic flooding of Egypt's Nile River submerged land and washed away boundary markers, there arose a need to re-measure and re-divide the land, and this gave rise to geometry. Hence the Latin word "geometria," from the Greek combination of the words for "earth" and "measurement," meaning land surveying. The work that brought ancient Greek geometric study to its culmination is the Greek Euclid's Elements.

notes.康丁斯基 (Wassily Kandinsky, 1866-1944) 出生於: Wassily Kandinsky (1866–1944) was born in Moscow, Russia, and is celebrated as the father of abstract expressionism — not only for his artistic creations, but also because he was a theorist of art, an aesthetic critic, and an educator, a rare combination in art history. His writings, such as 'Concerning the Spiritual in Art' and 'Point and Line to Plane,' are classic texts of modern art theory. His most vivid aesthetic idea was the "musical awakening of art" — perhaps shaped since childhood by classical music, Kandinsky drew much of his inspiration for using color from music: notes arranged with no apparent visual constraint may look freely scattered, yet in fact possess a strong inner logic and order, where the slightest deviation prevents the arrival at a state of "harmony." Thus Kandinsky's theory and practice sought to make color, line, and canvas resonate with the inner spirit. In his later work, he fused his early intuitive painting style with his later geometric style, adding fresh ideas to his art. He was a painter able to fuse color and music, allowing people to "listen" to painting and "paint" music. He said: "Colour is the keyboard, the eyes are the hammers, the soul is the piano with many strings. The artist is the hand that plays, touching one key or another, to cause vibrations in the soul."

His achievements in painting were brilliant; skilled at handling color, rich saturation and lively rhythm are among the hallmarks of his work, his paintings bright yet full of depth, joyful yet lyrical. Even before the war he already had considerable painting experience and achievement, and after the war he won the respect of the new generation with the same evergreen creative vitality. Although Liao Chi-chun's life passed through years of war and hardship and poverty, his brush painted a lyrical world that people long for. His art, like a dazzling seven-colored rainbow, transcended and magnificently bridged the gap between the old and new eras, striding boldly from the prewar past into the postwar present. (Material drawn from the Council for Cultural Affairs' "Taiwan Online Art Museum" website.)
Liao Chi-chun (1902–1976) had two works selected for the first Taiwan Fine Arts Exhibition (Taiten) in 1927, and the following year his painting "Courtyard with Banana Trees" was selected for the ninth Imperial Art Academy Exhibition (Teiten) in Japan, earning him recognition and acclaim in the art world — this became Liao's breakthrough work. The most eye-catching element of the painting is the banana tree standing upright in the foreground, tall, lush, and full of vitality. The daily life of village women at the corner of a house is set amid the shifting play of direct, refracted, and reflected sunlight, evoking the hazy atmosphere of a southern Taiwan summer. The dappled shadows of the trees, cast crosswise on the slanted ground and outer wall, carve out a sense of spatial depth. Liao used richly layered tones to depict how sunlight weaves among objects, bringing changing contrasts of light and shadow. In the hot summer, the banana trees appear ever more emerald green, contrasting with the fierce sunlight, while the reddish glow beneath the shade corresponds in rhythm to the sunlit white wall in the distance. This painting displays not only fluent and sensitive technique but also reflects the natural atmosphere and human warmth of southern Taiwan. The tones in the painting are strong yet harmonious, a style that persisted throughout his later works.
notes.張炳堂 (1928--2012) 台南人，14歲以一幅「大成坊」入選第7屆「台陽: Chang Ping-tang (1928–2012), a native of Tainan, was selected for the 7th Taiyang Exhibition at age 14 with his work 'Dacheng Gate,' becoming Taiwan's youngest painter at the time. He later studied under Guo Bochuan and was both mentor-student and friend with Liao Chi-chun and Yen Shui-long. Of an upright and unyielding character, he insisted on a native local cultural style and lived his whole life in Tainan. Perhaps because of southern Taiwan's blazing sunny weather, in his later years he used intense primary colors on canvas, bursting forth with the elemental power of sunlight and land, using concise lines and swift brushstrokes to paint, layer upon layer, the classical local beauty of Chihkan Tower, the Confucius Temple, the canal, and Anping Harbor. It could be said he "borrowed light from the sun to build the landscape of his heart, and returned the affection owed to his native land." Today, the brilliant red walls of temples and the vivid yellow and blue glazed tiles have become Chang's signature. Because of his bold red, vivid green, and deep blue color schemes, he has been called a leading figure of Taiwanese Fauvism, but a close look at the emotion in his brushwork also reveals the bold, unrestrained spirit of Expressionism.

David Livingstone (1813–1873), a Scotsman, devoted his life as both a doctor and a missionary to medical mission work among the peoples of Africa. He was also one of Africa's greatest explorers, discoverer of Victoria Falls and Lake Malawi, and was called the "Father of Africa." After his death, his heart was buried in African soil. Livingstone set off the wave of British overseas medical mission work, whose influence spread across the globe. Fellow Scotsmen, the Doctors Landsborough (David Landsborough III and David Landsborough IV, father and son), likewise moved by Livingstone's spirit, independently became medical missionaries and came to Taiwan, founding Changhua Christian Hospital. Over seventy years of medical mission work in Taiwan, they left behind the "love that touches the skin" and the "spirit of foot-washing," becoming a model of medical dedication in Taiwan and an exemplar of faith put into practice.

Mention Van Gogh, and one imagines a sky brilliant with stars; mention Monet, and a pond of shimmering water lilies comes to mind. Monet (Claude Monet, 1840–1926, French painter and one of the founders of Impressionism) dug an artificial pond beside his home at Giverny, not far from Paris, planted water lilies in it, and built a small Japanese-style bridge. Until the last twenty-some years of his life, Monet settled his body and spirit at this tranquil pond. Nearly all the subjects of his paintings were drawn from this pond garden. From different angles he painted the water lilies on the surface, the weeping willows by the pond, irises, and the old Japanese bridge. He continuously captured the changing light and color of the pond at different moments — dawn, dusk, after rain — composing a series of paintings from the blue sky and floating clouds, swaying willow branches, the curve of the wooden bridge, the water lilies on the pond, and the flowers and plants in the garden. In his later years, due to cataracts, his brushwork turned bolder and more expressive, and his canvases grew from small to large, some as large as seventeen meters wide. These water lily paintings from the end of Monet's life are rich in color and unrestrained in brushstroke, their shimmering colors flickering amid the reflections on the water. Monet painted more than 250 water lily paintings over his lifetime, now held in museums around the world. The Musée de l'Orangerie in Paris holds twelve large late-period water lily works by Monet.

A few years ago, returning to Taiwan, before dawn's first light my younger brother Meizhi and I drove south from Taichung to a hillside near Zhushan in Nantou, to capture the misty mountain sunrise. On the way back we visited Deshan Temple southwest of Zhushan. Deshan Temple, also known as Deshan Rock, was founded roughly during the Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty, nearly three hundred years ago. The Yunlin County Gazetteer records: "Deshan Rock lies twenty-eight li southeast of the county seat, embraced by mountains on all sides, with green trees and secluded bamboo groves reflecting each other, the sound of springs and birdsong, winding paths fragrant with flowers; looking all around, a vast expanse, with ranges of green peaks rising — truly a most extraordinary view." At the entrance to Deshan Temple stands a memorial archway, with a couplet reading: "How full is its virtuous work — the morning bell and evening drum open the path to enlightenment; to this mountain gate comes a Jia Dao — the sound of bamboo in the wind and pine mingles into verse." In front of the temple lies a crescent-shaped pond, its banks planted with mountain cherry, azalea, dragon juniper, and willow, with a grove of bamboo nearby casting its shade. It happened to be the Qingming season, and the vivid reds and purples, with rippling green shadows, were reflected on the water's surface. Behind the pond, before the main hall, lies a broad, quiet courtyard, all green as a carpet. Under the podocarpus trees to the left of the hall stands an inscribed stone, elegant and at ease. The surroundings of Deshan Temple are tranquil and pleasant, exuding a light and unhurried Zen atmosphere able to dissolve the cares of the bustling world. Ascending and gazing about, it seemed as though scenic wonders from every direction had gathered in this one place.
Leaving Deshan Temple, we took a quiet, gentle country road. The rice paddies, just transplanted with seedlings, mirrored the clouds and mountain colors, the whole vast plain a lush green. The village road once traveled by ox carts, the quiet villages, the meandering mountain ridges, the morning mist gradually dispersing... scenes of the old farming village rose unbidden before my eyes: on summer evenings, bare-chested farmers in small groups sitting on wooden benches outside a shop, old villagers puffing on cigarettes and chatting under the shade of trees, farmers shouldering their hoes walking home along the field paths, children carrying schoolbags returning home from school, the occasional bark of a dog echoing down the street... such moving scenes, giving off an air of peace and contentment. "Where the distant mountains meet the setting sun in a haze of mist, it seems as if this is the very place from which I once departed; at the river mouth, village children herd their calves home, and I rein in my horse to ask the way I once came." This poem, 'Mountain Journey,' by the early Qing woman poet Lin Yining, echoes the feeling of that moment.

Some consider this the most beautiful passage in the New Testament — "Consider the lilies of the field" is a phrase of far-reaching mood, rich in poetry. Jesus contrasts the lily with the glory of Solomon: the lily far surpasses the splendor upon Solomon's body, far surpasses everything Solomon possessed, far surpasses the temple he built and the land he ruled. notes.早期高醫許成章教授的中文課，有他講解的 \" 交點論 \" 以及學生提交的 \": In the early years, Professor Hsu Cheng-chang's Chinese class at Kaohsiung Medical College included his lectures on "the theory of intersecting points" and the students' assignments of writing "a single line of poetry." The theory of intersecting points was rich in philosophy and interpretation of life's chance encounters, carrying something of both fate and the butterfly effect: life seems to be made up of a chain of unexpected events, illogical turns, and unforeseen outcomes. The exercise of writing a single line of poetry, meanwhile, released our imagination and enriched the color of our thinking and the breadth of our vision. To have such a professor and such a humanistic education in freshman year meant that even our small Kaohsiung Medical campus was filled with an atmosphere and aspiration of freedom, vitality, and new beginnings. I still remember, during the lunch break, Professor Hsu lying sideways on the third-floor corridor of the library with his eyes covered, dozing off in a state of blissful contentment. Looking out from the third floor of the library was a stretch of rice paddies; the campus, with no surrounding wall, opened directly onto boundless fields, and on a clear day one could almost see Mount Banping in the distance — truly, "On a clear day one can see forever." Field after field of lush green was spring; field after field of golden rice ears was autumn. Call it a carefree, open-hearted feeling, or call it having one's ambitions set on the wide world — at the time, one's state of mind simply drifted with the wind; now, gathering it up, it all becomes poetry. The years flow on like water — Kaohsiung Medical College, how am I to seek you, to find you again?

'The Buddha Held Up a Flower, and Kasyapa Smiled'
The story of the Buddha holding up a flower and Kasyapa smiling comes from the first fascicle of the 'Compendium of the Five Lamps' (Wudeng Huiyuan). It records: the World-Honored One, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, held up a flower to show the congregation; at that time all the assembly remained silent, only the Venerable Kasyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: "I possess the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the formless form of reality, the subtle Dharma gate, not established on words, a special transmission outside the scriptures — I entrust it to Mahakasyapa."
What the Buddha transmitted was a state of mind supremely serene, tranquil, at ease, and wondrous — a state of mind pure and unstained, calm and open, free of desire and craving, unbound and unrestrained, at peace and self-content, unattached to appearances, transcending all things, abiding eternally with the world — a state of "formlessness" and "nirvana" at the highest level, which can only be intuited and understood, not expressed in words. And Kasyapa's slight smile was precisely because he had grasped this state, and so the Buddha transmitted the robe and bowl to him. The robe is the kasaya, the bowl is the alms bowl; robe and bowl together represent the orthodox lineage of the Buddhist Dharma.

During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, a man of Wuling made his living by fishing. Following a stream, he lost track of how far he had gone, when suddenly he came upon a grove of peach blossoms. For several hundred paces along both banks there were no other trees; the fragrant grass was fresh and beautiful, and fallen petals lay scattered about. The fisherman found this very strange, and went further, wishing to see the end of the grove. The grove ended where the stream began, and there he came upon a mountain with a small opening, through which a faint light seemed to shine. He left his boat and entered through the opening. At first it was very narrow, barely wide enough for a person to pass; after walking a few dozen more paces, it suddenly opened out into broad light. The land was level and open, the houses neat and orderly, with fine fields, beautiful ponds, and groves of mulberry and bamboo. Paths crossed in all directions, and the sounds of chickens and dogs could be heard from one another. The people coming and going, tilling the fields, men and women in their clothing, all appeared just like people from outside. The elderly with yellow hair and the children with hair in tufts were all joyful and content. Once the fisherman came out, he found his boat and retraced the way he had come, marking it at every point. On reaching the prefectural town, he went to see the governor and told him what he had found. The governor sent men to follow him and search for the marks he had left, but they became lost and never found the way again.
-- Eastern Jin. Tao Yuanming, 'Record of the Peach Blossom Spring'

From the figure portraits of his years studying in Japan, to the landscapes of the Sanxia stream during the Taiwan/Prefectural Exhibition period, to his postwar depictions of everyday popular life, his creative directions were diverse. Most of his subject matter was drawn from the scenery and people of his hometown Sanxia, conveying a natural, true, and warmly intimate feeling. In addition, Li Mei-shu devoted himself to local administration and oversaw the reconstruction of the Sanxia Zushi Temple, a task he pursued unwaveringly for decades, winning wide public affection and establishing an image as a patriarchal figure close to the people — a rarity among painters of his time. Despite his busy public duties, he never neglected his art, and actively participated in national exhibitions and the training of art talent, tirelessly promoting art education.

notes.松尾芭蕉 (1644-1694) ，是低級武土的兒子，1664年出版第一部俳諧詩:
Matsuo Basho (1644–1694) was the son of a low-ranking samurai. In 1664 he published his first collection of haikai poetry, and thereafter produced abundant work, primarily haiku; his widely recognized achievement was to bring the haiku form to its peak, earning him the title of Japan's Haiku Sage. In 1682 he began using "Basho" as his poetic name, and his hermitage was called the "Basho Hut." In 1689, at the age of 46, he set out from Edo (Tokyo) and traveled on foot through the deep interior of northern Honshu, covering 2,400 kilometers over half a year, and from what he saw, thought, and felt on this journey he wrote his enduring masterpiece 'Narrow Road to the Deep North' (Oku no Hosomichi), whose central theme is "sabi" (quiet solitude) and the sense of belonging between humans and nature.
The 'Narrow Road to the Deep North' lies in northeastern Honshu, Japan, and is a famous historic path; "oku" means the depths of the road, and "hoso" means a narrow, long path. Along the route Basho traveled, many stone monuments inscribed with his haiku remain.
Basho was deeply influenced by Zhuangzi, Tao Yuanming, Li Bai, Du Fu, Wang Wei, and other poets; his haiku encompass all things, and everywhere carry the essence and flavor of Tang and Song poetry. For example:
1. Into the tranquil old pond, a frog leaps in, a splash resounds.
2. In the utter stillness, a cicada's cry seeps into the rock.
3. Another year has passed in vain, still the same straw raincoat and sandals.
4. On the water bird's beak, a trace of white plum petal clings.
5. New moon in the east, setting sun in the west, a field of yellow rapeseed flowers.
A whole spring's sorrow waits to be washed away with wine,
a boat rocks on the river, a tavern banner beckons from above.
At Qiuniang's ferry and Tainiang's bridge,
the wind drifts on and on, the rain falls soft and thin.
When shall I return home to wash my traveler's robe,
to tune the silver-inlaid reed pipe, to burn incense shaped like the character "heart"?
The swift light of time so easily casts a person aside —
the cherries have reddened, the banana leaves have greened.
-- Southern Song. Jiang Jie, 'A Sprig of Plum Blossom'

'Scenery No. 2' is the most celebrated representative poem of Lin Heng-tai (b. 1924, from Beidou, Changhua, one of the founders of Li Poetry Journal). Formally, this poem strives for an avant-garde modernist technique, being a "visual poem" or "symbolic poem" expressed through the graphic arrangement of text. The poem uses repeated or parallel arrangements of lines or imagery to create an endless layering of space, an unbroken continuation of imagery. 'Scenery No. 2' uses plain language and simple imagery, but through the poet's distinctive handling of sentence patterns and the arrangement of the lines, the two simple images — windbreak forest and sea — produce a beauty of visual, musical, imaginative, and kinetic sense in poetry, expressing a subtle, modern, intellectual beauty of imagery — this is also why this poem has been so enduringly cited and discussed.

notes.柯錫杰 (1929-2020) 以「心象攝影」膾炙國際藝壇的攝影大師，被譽為「臺: Ko Si-chi (1929–2020), a master photographer celebrated internationally for his "psychological imagery photography," was hailed as "the first man of modern Taiwanese photography." Ko placed great importance on the conception and mood of photography; it is said that in order to capture a single photograph of the Aegean Sea, he waited a long time and finally pressed the shutter only once — and that photograph is 'Waiting for Venus.' Framing the sea, sky, and buildings, this work, with its simple, clear composition, reveals the photographer's calm, self-possessed elegance of quiet observation. Through simple compositional elements, it wondrously produces a combination of geometric forms; the three-dimensional depth is instantly dissolved, revealing a kind of illusory beauty within reality. The geometric forms arise from the distribution of different blocks of color, so that this tranquil scene appears almost like an abstract painting — its brilliant colors, sharply contrasted, condense the actual natural features of the scenery down to their barest minimum, becoming a pure dialogue of color. This work displays the "psychological imagery photography" style through which Ko led Taiwanese photographic expression in the 1970s and 1980s, using external scenery to lay out and express inner emotion, conveying through precise technique and aesthetic sense the literary "poetic mood" and the artistic "painterly texture." His photographic works using the "dye transfer" process greatly elevated the artistic level of color photography, drawing enormous response from the professional photography world. This series of works, when exhibited in Taiwan during this period, caused a sensation and had a profound influence on Taiwan's modern photography community.
notes.柯錫杰（1929年-- ），出生于台灣台南市，早年赴日學習攝影，返國後，以高度精: Ko Si-chi (1929– ), born in Tainan, Taiwan, went to Japan in his early years to study photography, and after returning home used highly precise imaging techniques to photograph portraits of figures such as the conductor Kuo Mei-chen and the dancer Huang Chung-liang, displaying a strong personal visual style and expressing the deep inner spirit of his subjects. In the 1960s he moved to New York, USA, becoming one of the few Asian photographers to gain recognition in the New York commercial photography world. In 1979, seeking a breakthrough in his personal artistic creation, Ko closed his New York studio and traveled alone, self-driving, through India, southern Europe, and North Africa for eight months, creating a distinctive style he called "psychological landscape." Through precise technique and aesthetic sense he conveyed the literary "poetic mood" and the artistic "painterly texture"; his photographic works using the "dye transfer" process greatly elevated the artistic level of color photography, drawing enormous response from the professional photography world. This series of works, when exhibited in Taiwan during this period, caused a sensation and had a profound influence on Taiwan's modern photography community, earning him the honorary title "the first man of modern Taiwanese photography." In 1993 he returned to settle permanently in Taiwan from New York, and together with his wife Fan Chieh-hsi founded the Chieh Hsi Chieh Dance Troupe. In 1994, the world-renowned Hammer Gallery in New York held his first photography exhibition. In 1996, he took part in an exhibition of color photography masters at the Lizan-Tops Gallery in New York. In 2000 and 2008, his representative work 'Waiting for Venus' was sold at Christie's and Ravenel auction houses respectively, each time setting a new record as the highest price ever paid for a photographic work by a Taiwanese artist.

The golden wheatfield, the dark, brooding sky, the dirt path stretching toward the horizon — all cut off abruptly by his brush, as if to say: let the human world reap its harvest, let there be no path left for himself. notes.梵谷是一位感情激動的畫家，一生充滿愛和熱情，充滿矛盾和悲劇。梵谷早期雖受荷蘭古畫: Van Gogh was a painter of intense feeling, whose life was filled with love and passion, contradiction and tragedy. Although Van Gogh's early work was influenced by the old Dutch masters and Impressionism, his era was also the time when Symbolism was rising — Symbolism sought to use color and form to interpret and evoke various hidden spiritual states. Contrasts of light and dark, and leaping colors, were a shared emotional undercurrent in modern poetry and art. Van Gogh's intense personal character was fully unleashed in his paintings — vivid colors, writhing, whirlpool-like burning brushstrokes, appropriately distorted subjects, and strong subjective vision. He poured not only spirit and emotion into his paintings but also emphasized the beauty of color and the symbolic significance of artistic expression, and in doing so foreshadowed the central theme of twentieth-century art: fundamental "purity."

Van Gogh's famous painting 'The Starry Night' is filled with lines of powerful force, one stroke following closely upon another, as strong and clear as the work of a sculptor. The upper two-thirds of the painting is a tranquil blue night sky. notes.棲蘭山檜木林處於中高海拔山區，此山域因峰高，谷深，雨霧足，形成孤島式的封閉性生態: The cypress forest of Qilan Mountain lies in a mid-to-high elevation mountain region; because the peaks are high, the valleys deep, and the rain and mist abundant, an isolated, enclosed ecological environment has formed here, allowing rare gymnosperms that grow alongside the cypress belt — such as the Taiwan yew, Taiwania, and Taiwan cedar, relict plants from the Arctic Tertiary period — to evolve, through long isolation, into species found only in Taiwan. These conifers, having gone through tens of millions of years of succession, may be called "living fossil trees," and hold a highly significant place in the study of ecological evolution. Because of the moist environment of Qilan Mountain, many plants grow in symbiosis with the cypresses; according to a survey by Professor Chen Yu-feng, as many as 82 species of epiphytic plants have been found on a single cypress tree. The name "Qilan" (meaning "roosting orchids") comes from the wild orchids that often cover the cypress trunks, creating a dreamlike scene. This area is called "Makauy" by the Atayal people, meaning mountain pepper. In 2002, after years of advocacy by civil forest conservation groups, the Ministry of the Interior announced the establishment of the "Makauy Cypress National Park" to protect the Qilan Mountain cypress forest. It was later suspended due to divergent views between government policy and indigenous concerns and rights, and remains under discussion today.

notes.極光的形成, 一方面與地球高層大氣和南北極磁埸的相互作用有關, 一方面與太陽噴: The formation of the aurora is related, on one hand, to the interaction between the Earth's upper atmosphere and the magnetic fields at the North and South Poles, and on the other hand, to the high-speed stream of charged particles ejected from the sun, generally called the solar wind. The solar wind is drawn in by the Earth's polar magnetic fields; the electrons it carries penetrate the magnetic field and enter the Earth's atmosphere, colliding with atoms or molecules of oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, helium, and other elements in the atmosphere, producing light of different colors. Aurora colors are generally whitish tinged with green, red, or yellow, varying in intensity, and their shapes are ever-changing and unpredictable — arcs, bands, curtains, flame-like forms, and so on. The stronger the solar storm (that is, the more sunspots on the sun's surface), the more charged particles it contains, and the more frequently the aurora appears, with more vivid coloring, and appearing at lower latitudes. The magnetic polar band at roughly 65–75 degrees north and south latitude is where the aurora most often appears; Fairbanks, Alaska, located at 64.8 degrees north latitude, is a good place to view the aurora borealis. In Churchill, in northern Canada, one can see polar bears as well as the northern lights.

notes.歐姬芙（Georgia O’Keeffe, 1887 ~ 1986），美國女畫家: Georgia O'Keeffe (1887–1986), American woman painter, renowned for her large-scale flower paintings, and remembered for the delicate yet abundant presence she left behind. Born in Wisconsin, USA, she resolved at age 12 to pursue painting. She studied art in Chicago, New York, and elsewhere. Drawn to solitary desert landscapes, she left her mark and imagery across the American Southwest, Texas, New Mexico, and other places, eventually settling in the wilderness near Santa Fe. The imagery appearing in O'Keeffe's works is consistently flowers, bones, and fragments of landscape, forming semi-abstract compositions — that is, a technique of "partial" representation — so that while she is difficult to classify as a purely abstract painter, her simplified planes of color, smooth and unadorned brushwork, and open, empty backgrounds are nonetheless close to the mood of abstract painting. Moreover, owing to her association with the "New York School," O'Keeffe's works have also become part of what represents American imagery. In addition, her works, whether landscapes or flowers, often incorporate forms suggestively evoking female anatomy. O'Keeffe disliked being called a "woman painter," insisting on being called simply a "painter"; given her sense of gender pride, it is quite possible that her paintings repeatedly celebrate feminine imagery and consciousness. O'Keeffe played a pivotal role in the American modernist movement, and many contemporary women admire and look up to her, prompted by her to reflect on the meaning of their own era as women. Many episodes of her life reveal why she became an idol followed and admired by contemporary women: a resilience and toughness of constant self-transformation, achieved through uncompromising self-healing and transcendence. And this beautiful vitality, in her paintings as in her person, has always existed quietly and deeply — just like the vast desert she loved.

notes.每年元宵節，台灣北部最具有民俗色彩的文化活動，平溪放天燈，也具有傳遞信息的歷史典:
Every year at the Lantern Festival, the release of sky lanterns at Pingxi is the folk cultural event with the richest local color in northern Taiwan, and it also carries a historical significance as a means of transmitting messages. During the Daoguang era of the Qing dynasty, early settlers moved from Hui'an, Anxi, and other places in Fujian into the upper reaches of the Keelung River, into the Shifenliao area (present-day Pingxi district). The villagers worked hard to cultivate the land, and the village prospered. Because the mountainous area was remote and beyond easy reach of the authorities, it became a haunt for bandits and outlaws. To save their lives, every year after the winter solstice the villagers would pack up their belongings and flee into the deep mountains for safety, only returning around the Lantern Festival, when able-bodied men would first go down the mountain to check whether it was safe, and once safety was confirmed, release sky lanterns to signal "all is well" and call the villagers back. From then on, the villagers of Shifenliao used the release of sky lanterns to celebrate the Lantern Festival, and to signal to neighboring villages that all was safe. Because of this the villagers there also call the sky lanterns "peace lanterns" or "blessing lanterns." An obscure, remote little village inherited this folk cultural tradition, which has continued unbroken for one or two hundred years, and has now become a major Lantern Festival celebration famous throughout Taiwan, even once voted by Discovery Channel as one of the world's top ten night festivals. Over the years it has drawn more than a hundred thousand visitors, earning the reputation of "sky lanterns in the north, bee fireworks in the south" (referring to the Yanshui Beehive Fireworks Festival). As the sky lanterns rise, so does hope rise again; through the sky lanterns people pray and make wishes, purify their hearts, weave dreams, and leave behind beautiful memories and experiences. Hu Erh-tai wrote a poem, 'Pingxi Sky Lanterns': "Nine-colored sky lanterns fly into the night sky, carrying ten thousand wishes up to the heavens; as stars fall beyond Pingxi, lingering hopes still remain within the heart."
In fact, the Hokkien pronunciation of "sky lantern" resembles that of "adding a son." In earlier times, settlers needed labor for land reclamation, and combined with the traditional agrarian society's preference for sons over daughters, a male child was seen as synonymous with labor and productivity. So people would pray at temples and release sky lanterns for blessings, often writing auspicious wishes on the lanterns such as "may a noble son be born soon" or "may the five grains bring a bountiful harvest." And since the Lantern Festival marks the beginning of the spring planting season, the early settlers released sky lanterns to report safety to their ancestors, and to pray to heaven for blessing and protection, hoping for the fulfillment of the year's wishes.

notes.無尾熊 ( Koala )，又稱爲樹熊, 不是熊類或鼠類, 是屬於有袋哺乳動物: The koala is not a bear or a rodent, but belongs to the marsupial mammals (Marsupialia), meaning that its young are carried and reared in the mother's pouch. The koala's pouch is located on its back, whereas in other marsupials such as the kangaroo or the possum, the pouch is on the front of the abdomen. Koalas are found mainly in the eucalyptus forests near the eastern coast of Australia, living on the leaves; Australia has more than 600 species of eucalyptus, but koalas eat only a few dozen of them. They live in the trees year-round, using their strong limbs and sharp claws to cling to branches, whether moving about or sleeping. Koalas are nocturnal animals, foraging at night and sleeping during the day, sometimes sleeping as long as 18 to 20 hours. During the day they choose a shady spot to rest, and visitors often find them drowsy and sleepy-eyed, adorably dozing without stirring no matter how long one waits. Australian Aboriginal peoples long ago observed that koalas rarely drink water, and named them "koala," meaning "no water." They were first discovered near the Blue Mountains outside Sydney in 1789; in the 19th century koalas were hunted in huge numbers, their population plummeting from a million to just a few thousand, prompting the Australian government to enact protective legislation and establish koala reserves for research and viewing.

A tree with a trunk one meter in diameter is at least 2,000 years old. Most grow at elevations above 3,400 meters, on mountains such as Yushan, Snow Mountain, and Mount Mabolasi. The most striking feature of the Yushan juniper is its extreme variation in form: in sheltered spots near the snow line it grows tall and upright as a proper tree, while above the snow line it becomes a low, creeping shrub. Growing mostly in harsh conditions on remote, high mountain peaks, and shaped by the ongoing torment of storms, sudden frost and snow cover, low temperatures, drought, and poor soil, its branches and trunk are eventually carved into twisted, contorted forms, hugging the ground and spreading low and wide, forming what is called a "dwarf mat shrubland" — like a bonsai sculpted by nature itself. The gnarled, entangled trunks are full of an unyielding, struggling vitality, bursting forth with boundless life force and resilience in Taiwan's high mountain wilderness, a sight that leaves viewers deeply moved.

notes.王攀元，國寳級畫家，1912生於江蘇，上海美術專科畢業，來台後任教於宜蘭羅東中學: Wang Pan-yuan, a national treasure-class painter, was born in 1912 in Jiangsu, graduated from the Shanghai Academy of Fine Arts, and after coming to Taiwan taught at Luodong High School in Yilan, where he and friends formed the 'Lanyang Painting Society.' He lived in seclusion on the Lanyang Plain for most of a century, and in 2001 received the 5th National Award for Arts, and in 2013 the 8th Kavalan Award. Orphaned young, Wang Pan-yuan used painting to reflect a lifetime of hardship; the youth of an orphan from a once-great family, and a life of turmoil and displacement, are both reflected in his work — his creations are, in effect, the crystallization of his life. Across variations on different themes, emptiness, simplicity, plainness, and distance remain the recurring undertone he lingers over — a soliloquy half-spoken and half-withheld, a solitary resentment now visible, now hidden. His pictures, both concrete and abstract, both simple and profound, contain within them a rich philosophy of life. Because of his distinctively transcendent style, he has been called "the poet of the canvas."

Maya civilization is an ancient civilization distributed across the tropical rainforests of what are today five Central American countries: the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Belize. Although it remained at a Neolithic technological stage, it achieved extremely high accomplishments in architecture, astronomy, mathematics, agriculture, art, and writing. Together with the Inca Empire of South America and the Aztec Empire of Mexico, it is ranked as one of the three great civilizations of the Americas. Unlike other ancient civilizations — such as the civilization of the two rivers in Babylon, the Nile civilization of Egypt, the Yellow River civilization of China, and the Ganges civilization of India — Maya civilization did not originate along a great river basin, but arose independently within the tropical rainforest, and so is called a "jungle civilization."
According to the Mesoamerican chronology, Maya civilization is divided into the Preclassic, Classic, and Postclassic periods. The Preclassic period (1500 BC – 300 AD), also called the formative period, saw the invention of the calendar and writing system, the erection of monuments, and the construction of buildings. The Classic period was the golden age (4th–9th century), when pyramid and temple architecture, astronomy, the calendar, and art all reached their height. In the Postclassic period (9th–16th century), city-states migrated from south to north into the Yucatan Peninsula, and the culture gradually declined. Unlike other ancient civilizations such as Egypt, China, or Greece and Rome, the Maya never possessed a single unified powerful empire; at its height, Maya civilization was dispersed among hundreds of city-states, yet the language, writing, religious beliefs, and traditional customs of the various city-states still belonged to the same cultural sphere.
Beginning in the 9th century AD, the city-states of the Classic-period Maya civilization suddenly and simultaneously fell into decline; by the 10th to 11th centuries, the once-flourishing Maya city-states had all been abandoned and were reclaimed by the jungle. By the time Columbus reached the American continent in 1492, the Maya region was already in a state of fragmentation. In the 16th century, the Aztec Empire, inheritor of Maya culture, was destroyed by the Spanish. Why the advanced civilization the Maya created during the Classic period suddenly disappeared remains, to this day, without a definitive explanation. The last stone stele in the entire Maya region was completed in the year 909, when the construction of towers and temples also stopped, the population dispersed rapidly, and the wisdom of its people was exhausted. Many explanations have been offered for this mystery of disappearance, such as invasion by other peoples, epidemic disease, climate change, popular uprisings, and competition among city-states for resources. Recent geological research at the Great Blue Hole off the coast of Belize has revealed that the disappearance of Maya civilization may be related to a century-long great drought around the 10th century.
The lost city-states are scattered across the Maya region of Central America; after a thousand years, only a small number of large pyramids, temples, monumental steles, and plazas have been excavated and restored, while most ruins remain buried beneath the jungle's trees, and smaller ones lie hidden beneath mounds of earth and grass. In the minds of Maya enthusiasts, the five great Maya sites are:
1. Tikal, the largest Maya city-state (Guatemala).
2. Copan, known as the "Athens of the New World" (Honduras).
3. Palenque (Mexico), whose pyramid tomb contains the stone-carved sarcophagus lid rumored to depict "a Maya astronaut piloting a spacecraft."
4. Uxmal (Mexico), with its complete layout and magnificently carved reliefs.
5. Chichen Itza (Mexico), near Cancun, thronged with tourists for its Temple of the Feathered Serpent and observatory.

Bai Ling, essay, 'The Tamsui That Belongs to the Taiwanese Painter Chen Cheng-po,' April 2014
Few who have visited Taipei have not also gone to Tamsui. But the Tamsui of today seems almost a different place from the Tamsui I saw at twenty, and what I saw is clearly also quite different from the Tamsui in Chen Cheng-po's painting 'Tamsui at Sunset.' This painting sold for NT$215 million at a Hong Kong international auction in 2007, setting the record price for an oil painting by a Taiwanese artist. The scenery in this painting appears as if viewed from the air, from the height of a 30-story building; the Tamsui River lies on the left, flowing from the bottom of the picture upward, its area widening and its scale growing ever more expansive; a row of Chinese-style old houses with red tiles and white walls winds upward from the bottom toward the distance, rising and falling in gentle, gradually diminishing motion, accompanied by the Western-style Mackay Memorial Church and scattered patches of green shade, stretching all the way to the top of the painting, until it meets the sea horizon beneath the light of the setting sun, almost converging with the distant Fort San Domingo (Hongmao Cheng). The composition is remarkable, its colors as if brilliant pigments had been poured down from the whole sky; a red glow of sunset light suffuses the entire canvas, leaving the viewer in a state of blissful, expansive ease. Chen Cheng-po's Tamsui series numbers at least ten paintings, preserving the fewest Japanese-style elements, with only Fujian-style and European-style architecture breathing and interacting with one another — this is the Tamsui town that belongs to Chen Cheng-po. This Tamsui belonging to Chen Cheng-po was forged together from the old houses, the setting sun, and Chen Cheng-po's passionate brush. With this single painting alone, old Tamsui has been rendered immortal.
Chen Cheng-po (1895–1947), a painter born in Chiayi, Taiwan, had his work 'Outside Chiayi Street' selected for Japan's Imperial Art Academy Exhibition in 1926, making him the first Taiwanese to enter a Japanese official exhibition with a Western-style painting. He was subsequently selected for the Imperial Exhibition several more times. During the 228 Incident of 1947, he was arrested by Nationalist government troops, publicly humiliated, and shot in front of Chiayi Railway Station. Chen Cheng-po's life spanned the modern art movements of Taiwan, Tokyo, and Shanghai, and he holds a pivotal, representative place in art history; his paintings overflow with passion for his homeland and his era, presenting through their imagery the customs and character of Taiwan in the early twentieth century, and the complex process by which Taiwanese art entered modernity. His rich, vivid, and tragic life reflects the twists and turns experienced by Taiwan's art history under different ruling regimes, and is also a historical microcosm of the modernization process of modern East Asian art.
notes.皮特·蒙德里安（Piet Mondrian，1872－1944），荷蘭畫家，抽象: Piet Mondrian (1872–1944), Dutch painter, a central figure of abstract De Stijl painting and one of the founders of non-representational art, called his own style "Neoplasticism," also known as "geometric abstraction." He had great influence on later architecture, design, and other fields. The three painters who each founded their own school in Dutch art history are Rembrandt in the 17th century, Van Gogh in the 19th century, and Mondrian in the 20th century. Picasso's abstraction and Rembrandt's cubism were the mentors of Mondrian's stylistic transformation; Mondrian ultimately drew the essence from the two, using abstract forms and neutral colors to convey his ideas of order and peace. For Mondrian, all things in nature — whether mountains and water, trees, or houses and buildings — could be reduced to pure lines and blocks of color. He once said: "Looking at the sea, the sky, and the stars, I represent them through a great many crosses. The grandeur of nature deeply moved me; I try to express that sense of vastness, tranquil harmony, and unity."

notes.祈福的天燈，除了民俗文化，感性的意義之外，背後還有精準的科學原理。天燈之所以會浮: Behind the sky lantern's blessing — beyond its folk-cultural and emotional significance — lies a precise scientific principle. The reason a sky lantern rises is based on the principle of buoyancy, namely "Archimedes' principle of buoyancy," which states that "the buoyant force an object experiences in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid it displaces, and whether it sinks or floats depends on density: an object denser than the fluid sinks, while one less dense floats." The main actor in the sky lantern's rise is gas. Before being heated, the air inside and outside the lantern is identical; once heated, the air inside the lantern expands, and soon the lantern can no longer contain all the expanding air molecules, so the excess air escapes from the lantern, reducing its mass. Since density equals mass divided by volume, and the volume stays the same while the mass decreases, the density of the air inside the lantern decreases, and the lantern gently rises. A hot-air balloon carrying passengers works on the same principle. A lantern flying toward the sky will only begin to descend once the kerosene-soaked paper at its base has burned out. When a whole cluster of sky lanterns is released together, rising one after another into the sky, it is truly a dazzling sight to behold. As the lanterns drift away on the wind, they look like meteors trailing fire crossing the night sky, and finally the lanterns dissolve into points of starlight, gradually vanishing into the deep night.

notes.米勒 ( Jean-Francois Millt,1814-1875)，法國巴比: Millet (Jean-Francois Millet, 1814–1875), painter of the French Barbizon School, renowned for his realistic depictions of rural customs and peasant life, is considered France's greatest painter of rural life. Romain Rolland, in his biography of Millet, wrote: "Millet, this classical master who poured his whole spirit into the eternal rather than the fleeting moment, was unlike any other painter in the grand and magnificent feeling and expression he gave to the earth to which all things return." His famous painting 'The Angelus' (also called 'Evening Prayer') depicts two farming spouses who, upon hearing the evening bell, bow their heads in devout prayer. In the distance, a church spire rises over the fields at dusk, the two figures' silhouettes set against the backdrop of the fading evening light. Although 'The Angelus' begins from a depiction of natural scenery, the postures of the two figures, under the painter's brush, seem to celebrate the blessings nature bestows upon humankind and the humble, grateful submission of human beings. Millet, in an intimate pictorial language, faithfully reflects the hard toil and self-sufficient gratitude of peasant daily life. This painting is a treasured holding of the Musee d'Orsay in Paris. His other representative works include 'The Gleaners,' 'The Sower,' and 'The Shepherdess.'
notes.米羅 ( Joan Miro 1893–1983 ) 是西班牙三大畫家之一，和: Joan Miro (1893–1983) is one of the three great Spanish painters, alongside Picasso and Dali. Using a surrealist approach and simplified imagery, he expressed a dreamlike, poetic quality. His paintings are filled with whimsy, unpredictability, and humor. Combined with distorted animals, deformed organic shapes, and unusual geometric constructions, his works stand out as distinctive. His bright, rich colors — especially blue, red, yellow, green, black, and blank space — along with sharp lines, dots, and patterns, construct amorphous, amoeba-like shapes. Miro's style always carries a sense of innocence, purity, and playfulness. Using simple marks and unadorned elements, he achieved a realm of free expression in modern painting; although his works are fantastical and mysterious, their expression is clear, filled with metaphor, humor, and lightness, expressing a childlike simplicity and innocence, and rich in poetry. He held that the mystery expressed in painting must be grounded in concrete natural forms. Miro was a Surrealist painter who sought to destroy the dominance of reason and logic, releasing the impulses of the unconscious and illogical mind, and probing the mysteries of the invisible realm and the visual world.

notes.綠島人權文化園區位於將軍岩前方，涵蓋人權紀念公園，綠洲山莊，莊敬營區，綠島技能訓: The Green Island Human Rights Culture Park is located in front of General Rock, encompassing the Human Rights Memorial Park, Oasis Villa, Zhuangjing Camp, the Green Island Vocational Training Center, and Swallow Cave, among others. Oasis Villa was the site where political prisoners and prisoners of conscience were held during the White Terror period. It preserves the once-towering perimeter walls, barbed wire, exercise yard, auditorium, and the Bagua Building (the prison block, so named because, viewed from above, the building resembles the eight trigrams). Inside the villa many materials related to the White Terror period are on display. The prison cells of the Bagua Building are narrow and oppressive, shrouded in a dim, heavy atmosphere that, even now, many years later, has never quite lifted. The Green Island Human Rights Memorial Park was designed by the renowned Taiwanese architect Han Pao-teh and was formally opened on December 10, 2002, World Human Rights Day. The white exterior of the building carries an image of peace, symbolizing a formal farewell to the "White Terror era" and a step into a new age of democracy and justice. The design of the monument sinking into the ground (note: the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C., designed by the Chinese-American architect Maya Lin, is likewise a structure that sinks into the earth) symbolizes the bleak history buried in the shadows of archival documents, the injustice of being ignored and discriminated against, and the suffering and humiliation that could never be redressed. The elongated Human Rights Memorial, also known as the "Monument of Tears," is inscribed with the names of former political prisoners and the dates of their imprisonment. Along the spiraling sloped walkway, when it rains, rainwater flows through channels on either side into the Pool of Tears, symbolizing the tears shed by the prisoners' families and by all the people of Taiwan on their behalf. Along the coast of the Human Rights Memorial Park stand General Rock and Three Peaks Rock, black reef formations jutting out from the headland that resemble a general clad in armor together with three standing soldiers. From here one can also gaze out at Oxhead Mountain, making this a landmark that combines both historical significance and natural scenery.

notes.艾爾斯岩 ( Ayers Rock ) 位於澳洲大陸中部，像一座突破時空天界的巨:
Ayers Rock is located in the center of the Australian continent, standing like a colossal monument breaking through space and time, rising in solitary grandeur from the boundless red desert. With a circumference of 9 kilometers and an elevation of 867 meters (348 meters above the surrounding ground), it is the largest single freestanding rock in the world and one of Australia's most extraordinary natural wonders. To this day scientists have not conclusively determined how it was formed — theories range from it being a fallen meteorite, like an iceberg with only its tip showing above the surface, to it being uplifted seabed sediment, the hard remnant rock left behind after eons of weathering and erosion. Whatever the case, this great red rock has been called Australia's red heart, the navel of the earth.
The Aboriginal peoples of Australia call this giant rock "Uluru," meaning "a place of meeting and gathering" — it is Mother Earth, a symbol of the creation of all things, and a sacred site where one may commune with the spirits of one's ancestors. In 1987 it was designated "Uluru National Park" and placed on the World Natural Heritage list; it is now managed entirely by the Aboriginal Anangu people. The Western name "Ayers Rock" dates back to 1873, when a European geological surveyor first discovered the formation and named it after Sir Henry Ayers, then Chief Secretary (Governor) of South Australia.
Like the boundless wilderness and sand that surround it, Uluru's rock is rich in iron ore, and its surface appears red due to oxidation. As the angle of the sun changes and the density of the air shifts, the rock's surface takes on different colors. At sunrise and sunset, Uluru's colors are at their most astonishing and magnificent, shifting from orange-yellow to pale red, then to deep purples and reds, set against a faintly lavender-blue sky, as if it were a blazing flame standing apart from the world. As night falls, it withdraws quietly into the black earth in a tawny silhouette, radiating an ancient mystery beneath the starry sky.

The Jasmine Revolution (Révolution de jasmin) refers to the anti-government demonstrations in Tunisia, North Africa, from late 2010 to early 2011, which led to the collapse of the ruling regime. It takes its name from jasmine, Tunisia's national flower. It was the first revolution among Arab nations in which a popular uprising toppled the ruling government. The Jasmine Revolution's model of protest was emulated by people in other countries such as Algeria and Egypt, and in the following months a wave of anti-government demonstrations spread across North Africa and the Middle East. Tunisia subsequently established a transitional government and became the only country of the Jasmine Revolution to achieve a democratic transition.
The Sunflower Movement refers to the student-led occupation of the Legislative Yuan's main chamber beginning March 18, 2014, in opposition to the Kuomintang's unilateral move to have the Cross-Strait Service Trade Agreement declared as merely 'filed for reference' rather than substantively reviewed. At the same time, students and members of the public from all over Taiwan flocked to the Legislative Yuan in support, and the momentum surged, eventually developing into what became known as the Sunflower Generation student movement. Its effects included the 2016 change in ruling party and the rise of the New Power Party, among others.
The Yulan flower, also known as bailan, baiyulan, or 'flower that longs for spring,' gets its name 'yulan' (jade orchid) because its buds, when opening, resemble a jade wine cup rising above the branch, and its subtle fragrance recalls that of an orchid. In earlier times, women often wore the blossoms as hair ornaments or pinned them to their lapels — both beautiful to look at and pleasantly fragrant — and they have long been beloved by the people of Taiwan. Having crossed the ocean to Taiwan hundreds of years ago, the yulan flower has long been woven into the daily life and affections of ordinary people, becoming one of the flowers most representative of Taiwan's local beauty. The yulan favors heat and humidity; the largest production areas for yulan in Taiwan are Gaoshu Township and Yanpu Township in Pingtung County.
