notes.董陽孜（1942年10月6日－）台灣書法藝術家。1942年出生上海、十歲來台，大: Tong Yang-Tze (born October 6, 1942) is a Taiwanese calligraphy artist. Born in Shanghai in 1942, she came to Taiwan at age ten and studied in the Fine Arts Department of National Taiwan Normal University, where during her studies she sought guidance from painters and calligraphers including Zhang Guyan, Ding Nianxian, Tai Jingnong, Zhang Longyan, and Fu Shen. After graduating she went to the United States to further her artistic training, studying in the Art Department of the University of Massachusetts (1966–1968), majoring in oil painting with a minor in ceramics. After graduating in 1970 she worked in graphic design in New York, and during her years in the U.S. won a national creative design competition's cover design award. After returning to settle in Taiwan in 1977, she devoted herself to calligraphic creation. In her early period she favored the regular script of Yan Zhenqing and the style of Northern Wei steles; in recent years she has leaned toward the calligraphic sensibility of Wang Xizhi and Huaisu, incorporating Western compositional theory into her work, blending the aesthetics of modern graphic design with traditional calligraphy. From roughly 2002 to 2018, some fifteen years, Tong Yang-Tze, building on her established style, explored large-scale works. Her sweeping, monumental calligraphy challenges the audience's experience of viewing calligraphic art. "Monumental writing poses a challenge, quite different from traditional calligraphy, for both the artist's creative process and the audience's viewing experience. The artist's writing shifts from being created at a desk to being a spatial movement within an environment; the large scale of the work creates an environmental, immersive viewing experience for the audience, transforming the traditional relationship between work and viewer." As one of Taiwan's leading calligraphy artists, Tong Yang-Tze, even past the age of seventy, remains tireless in her creative work. In recent years she has not only worked across disciplines, collaborating with contemporary music and dance, but hopes, through the interpretation of different modes of writing, to pass the beauty of textual line and calligraphic expression on to a new generation, conveying the aesthetics of East Asian script.

Salvador Dalí (1904–1989) was a towering master of 20th-century Surrealism, and Spain's celebrated pioneer of Impressionism, Cubism, Dadaism, and eccentric abstract art. Dalí was a supremely versatile artist, well-versed in physics, chemistry, mathematics, philosophy, aesthetics, and science. Few artists have engaged so directly with such a wide and complex range of subjects; historians of world art consider him the "all-round genius" after Leonardo da Vinci, and he is internationally recognized as the most "surreal" of Spanish artists. Over a creative career spanning sixty years, he produced countless astonishing, jaw-dropping works, among which one of the most familiar — and one that Dalí himself continually questioned and drew inspiration from — is his 1931 work "The Persistence of Memory," also known as "The Soft Watches." Critics have endlessly debated the meaning embedded in the work, offering a wide range of interpretations; although Dalí himself gave some explanation of the painting's origins, this has not helped viewers unlock the puzzle within it. But whatever its original meaning — or perhaps it has none at all — this powerful and deeply moving painting can rightly be regarded as a classic of Surrealism.
"In frozen time, memory endures. In soft time, art transcends, surpassing the limits of the visible."

Marc Chagall (1887–1985) was a deeply emotional and romantic painter and poet. Born into a humble, traditional Jewish farming family in Vitebsk, Russia, he lived through the Russian Revolution and two world wars; the turmoil of war, compounded by his Jewish identity, gave him a keen sense of the unpredictability of worldly affairs and of his own inborn cultural destiny. All these swirling, shifting emotions found expression in his paintings. Beyond his homeland, Jewish culture, and love, Chagall produced throughout his life many dreamlike paintings. Entering a Chagall painting feels like stepping into a fantastical world. He treated things with humor, fantasy, and an unconscious quality, giving his works a poetic sensibility and another layer of aesthetic meaning. Given the content and direction of his work, art historians classify him within Surrealism or a "supernatural" style. Yet others feel his distinctive painting style belongs to no school at all — he belongs only to himself.
Figure 1: "The Birthday," 1915. Museum of Modern Art, New York.
Beyond painting, Chagall is well known for his rich emotional life. Apart from his various romances in his youth, the great love of his life was undoubtedly his first wife, Bella. For Bella, Chagall created more than thirty paintings expressing his sincere, enduring feelings for her. "She has soared above my canvases for years, guiding my creation," Chagall said. In art history, painters who take pure romantic love between a man and a woman as their central subject can be counted on one hand, yet Chagall painted deeply loving works centered on himself and his wife Bella; given Chagall's stature in art history combined with the dreamlike sentiment in these paintings, he is undoubtedly a romantic and deeply sincere artist.
Figure 2: "I and the Village," 1911. Museum of Modern Art, New York.
The kaleidoscope of memories all appear together in this painting depicting his hometown of Vitebsk. Although Chagall spent only a few short years of his life in his hometown, the images of those days were deeply etched in his mind; he used painting to express the nostalgia and longing he felt in his heart for his hometown and the Russian countryside. In many of his other works, scenes of rural life, cows, horses, chickens, and pigeons often appear as well, showing just how strong his ties to his Russian homeland were.

notes.詹姆斯·庫克（James Cook，1728年－1779年），人稱庫克船長（Ca: James Cook (1728–1779), known as Captain Cook, was a British Royal Navy officer, navigator, explorer, and cartographer. He commanded three voyages to the Pacific Ocean, was among the first Europeans to land on the eastern coast of Australia and the Hawaiian Islands, and was the first to sail a European ship completely around New Zealand. Over thousands of kilometers of Pacific voyaging, he ventured deep into regions previously unknown to the West. Using a theodolite, he produced numerous accurate maps of the islands between New Zealand and Hawaii. In the course of his explorations, Cook also named many newly discovered islands and features. Across his voyages he displayed a combination of navigational skill, surveying and mapmaking ability, resilience in adversity, and leadership in crisis management. In 1779, during his third Pacific expedition, he was killed in a clash with islanders in Hawaii. Cook made major contributions to nautical science and geography that continued to influence the field into the 20th century, and monuments and statues have been erected in many places to honor his achievements. quietly I wave, bidding farewell to the clouds in the western sky.

their reflections shimmering on the waves stir within my heart.

"Landscape No. 2" is the most celebrated representative work of Lin Heng-tai (1924– , born in Beidou, Changhua, one of the founders of the Li Poetry journal). Formally, this poem is dedicated to experimenting with avant-garde modernist techniques, presenting a 'pictorial poem' or 'symbolic poem' arranged through the visual layout of text. The poem uses the repetition or parallel arrangement of lines or imagistic phrases to create an infinite layering of space, an unending extension of imagery. "Landscape No. 2" uses plain language and simple imagery, but through the poet's distinctive syntactic treatment and the arrangement of its lines, the two simple sets of images — windbreak forest and sea — produce a poetic beauty of vision, music, imagination, and speed, expressing a subtle, modern intellectual beauty of imagery. This is why the poem continues to be cited and discussed.

These three lines of poetry convey a sense of utter solitude, yet also a humble and graceful persistence. They fuse Eastern Zen philosophy with Western modern sensibility, creating a dialogue across time and space.
1. The end of the road: "Walking to where the water ends"
This line is drawn from Wang Wei's "My Retreat at Mount Zhongnan": "I walk to where the water ends, and sit and watch the clouds rise."
Literal meaning: Walking to the very source of the water, the path disappears, and the water itself vanishes.
Deeper metaphor: This represents a dead end, or a turning point in life. In the traditional poem, the next line is usually "and sit and watch the clouds rise," representing an open-minded acceptance of whatever comes. But in this poem, the poet does not turn toward serene clouds — instead turns toward the "wind."
2. The object of address: "speaking to the wind"
Instability: Wind cannot be grasped — it is flowing and formless. Speaking to the wind implies that there is no longer anyone nearby to listen, or that the one the poet appeals to is, like the wind, liable to leave at any moment.
A posture of solitude: To open one's mouth to the empty wind at the very place the water ends is an image of utter desolation.
3. The core plea: "Keep me in the picture"
This is a thoroughly modern English phrase that breaks the classical mood established by the first two lines, producing a striking impact:
A longing to be remembered: "Keep me in the picture" originally means "let me know too" or "don't leave me out." Here it feels more like a plea: even as the world changes and you move on, please keep a place for me somewhere in the blueprint of your life.
The desire to be fixed in place: Having walked to where the water ends, the poet feels the fear of vanishing. Unwilling to be forgotten, he begs the wind — the only thing still moving — to preserve his image.
Summary and mood
This poem depicts a state of mind that refuses to let go even at the very end of the road.
It transforms Wang Wei's Zen spirit of 'accepting what comes' into a modern person's anxiety and longing for a sense of existence. Standing at the desolate end of the road, facing the wind — which is bound to leave (perhaps representing a lover, time, or fate) — the poet humbly pleads: "Please do not erase my presence from your world."
It is a beautiful yet heartbreaking kind of stubbornness.
The poem itself is like a soft whisper carried on the wind — well worth savoring.
notes.野柳女王岩究竟有多少歲數 ? 女王岩在地殼變動的過程中，因受海水風吹差別浸蝕而: How old is the Queen's Head Rock at Yehliu, really? The Queen's Head took on its present form gradually through crustal movement and differential erosion by sea and wind. Given that its highest point does not exceed 8 meters above sea level, and calculating with a northern Taiwan coastal uplift rate of 2 to 4 millimeters per year, it would have taken less than 5,000 years for the rock to rise to its current height since it first emerged above the surface and began to be subject to erosion by seawater. So the Queen's Head is no more than 5,000 years old. Owing to years of erosion by sea, wind, sun, rain, and human touch, its 'neck' has grown steadily thinner. In 1994 the neck circumference of the 'Queen's Head' was about 220 cm; by 2012 it was about 130 cm; by 2018 about 125 cm — compared to 138.27 cm in 2008, it shrank by 20 cm over ten years, and compared to 220 cm thirty-one years earlier, it has shrunk by 103.41 cm. An actual measurement taken in October 2024 put the neck circumference at 116.59 cm. Based on the average annual rate of shrinkage from natural weathering over the years — roughly 0.2 to 0.5 cm per year — it is estimated that the Queen's Head Rock has only ten to twenty more years remaining before it collapses.

George Leslie MacKay (March 21, 1844 – June 2, 1901), also known by his Chinese name Kai Jai-Li, is commonly called Dr. MacKay in recognition of his achievements in missionary work, for which he received an honorary doctorate in theology; ordinary Taiwanese nicknamed him the 'Black-Bearded Barbarian.' He was Canada's first overseas missionary. In March 1872 he landed at Hobe (present-day Tamsui), choosing this location as his base for missionary, medical, and educational work in Taiwan. Over nearly thirty years, he not only spread the Christian faith and established the Presbyterian Church in northern Taiwan, but the hospitals and schools he founded also became milestones in Taiwan's modernization, making a profound contribution to enlightening the public, opening up new ways of thinking, and transforming social customs. He made Tamsui his home, married and raised children there, and lived among ordinary people; after his death he was buried at Hobe Fort in Tamsui. His remarkable life brought rich cultural experience to northern Taiwan, and his love for and identification with Taiwan continues to inspire the people of Taiwan today.

notes.黑色是「火所熏之色也」。從現代光譜學的色彩理論來看，黑色是由於光線照射在物體上時: Black is "the color produced by smoke from fire." From the perspective of modern spectral color theory, black results when light striking an object is entirely absorbed by that object — it is the terminus of all chromatic colors. White is "the color of the West, associated with yin." It results when an object absorbs none of the light striking it, instead reflecting all of it back to our eyes — it is thus the sum of all colors in the spectrum, the source of all colors. Black and white are the two extremes of color: white represents the extreme presence of light, releasing every color; black represents the extreme absence of light, swallowing every color. All color perceived by the eye begins at white and ends at black. In modern color theory, both black and white lack hue and saturation, differing only in brightness. Even so, the expressive richness they convey is in no way inferior to the chromatic colors — equally full of variation and countless forms. (Daily Headlines: January 7, 2017)

notes.龜山島，又稱龜山嶼，最早的名字叫煙斗嶼，頭城人常稱爲龜島或龜嶼。位於宜蘭蘭陽平原: Turtle Island, also called Guishan Islet, was originally named Pipe Islet; residents of Toucheng commonly call it Turtle Island or Turtle Islet. Located in the Pacific Ocean off the eastern side of the Lanyang Plain in Yilan, it takes its name from its resemblance to a floating turtle. Because the coastline of the Lanyang Plain curves, Turtle Island's apparent shape changes depending on the viewer's location — sometimes the whole turtle appears to lie flat on the water's surface (as seen from around Toucheng and Beiguan), sometimes only the turtle's body is visible, and sometimes it appears triangular (as seen from around Luodong and Wujie) — giving rise to the vivid phrase 'the turtle turns its head.' Turtle Island is a volcanic island isolated offshore, composed mainly of two volcanic bodies forming the turtle's head and horn, while the turtle's tail is a long, narrow sandbar that shifts with the tides, like a turtle swishing its tail. Tens of thousands of years ago the island experienced volcanic eruptions, and sulfur vents and hot springs remain on the island today. In addition, four kilometers southwest of Turtle Island lies an even smaller islet called 'Turtle Egg Islet.' With its ever-changing appearance, Turtle Island has always kept watch over the Lanyang Plain, and has been intertwined with the lives of the people of Yilan since ancient times, forming part of their spiritual life. Before weather forecasting existed, whether clouds gathered atop Turtle Island served as the compass by which the people of Yilan judged the weather. Through the lenses of photographers, the brushes of painters, the ingenuity of designers, and the writing of literary figures, people continue to uncover the rich vitality of Turtle Island. In Taiwan, most people's knowledge of "Lupin Flower" derives from the novelist Zhong Zhaozheng's 1961 novel of the same name, and it became widely known after the novel was made into a moving film in 1989. Zhong Zhaozheng used the blooming and falling of the lupine flower as a metaphor for the swift decline of a gifted child, and also as a metaphor for certain problems facing Taiwan's education system at the time. In the film's theme song "Lupin Flower," the line about 'the tea garden back home is full of blossoms' refers to the lupine flower. The lupine's scientific name, 'Lupin,' originally means 'bitterness' in Greek; its seeds are extremely bitter, and anyone who mistakenly eats them shows an expression of suffering — hence the flower's language also carries connotations of 'sorrow.' The lupine belongs to the pea family, with many varieties and vividly colored blossoms; the lupine grown as green manure in Taiwan's tea gardens is the yellow-flowered lupine. From sowing, growth, to flowering and fruiting, its cycle coincides exactly with the tea plants' winter dormancy, making it the ideal green manure crop for tea gardens. Every March is lupine blooming season, when clusters of bright yellow flowers rise upward, adding much color to the tea garden scenery. The film "Lupin Flower" won multiple awards, including at the 26th Golden Horse Awards and the Special Humanitarian Award at the 40th Berlin International Film Festival.

notes.In physic, mass–energy equivalence state:
In physic, mass–energy equivalence states that anything having mass has an equivalent amount of energy and vice versa, with these fundamental quantities directly relating to one another by Albert Einstein’s famous formula:     E=MC2{\displaystyle E=mc^{2}}
This formula states that the equivalent energy (E) can be calculated as the mass (m) multiplied by the speed of light (c = ~3×108 m/s) squared. Similarly, anything having energy exhibits a corresponding mass m given by its energy E divided by the speed of light squared c2. Because the speed of light is a very large number in everyday units, the formula implies that even an everyday object at rest with a modest amount of mass has a very large amount of energy intrinsically. Chemical, nuclear, and other energy transformations may cause a system to lose some of its energy content (and thus some corresponding mass), releasing it as the radiant energy of light or as thermal energy for example.                         ( Wikipedia )

Kom Ombo is located about thirty kilometers south of Aswan, an ancient city on the banks of the Nile. 'Kom' means gold and 'Ombo' means mountain, so Kom Ombo means 'Gold Mountain.' It was the site of ancient Egypt's capital of gold, and the golden objects used in the royal court, burial goods, and coffins of ancient Egypt all came from here. Where the Nile bends at this point, fierce crocodiles were once common, and the ancient Egyptians worshipped the crocodile as a god.
The Temple of Kom Ombo was built around 180-145 BC and was expanded and added to by successive rulers over the generations. Over the long centuries, due to flooding of the Nile, earthquakes, and plundering, the temple fell into ruin. Restoration work did not begin until the late nineteenth century. The Temple of Kom Ombo is the only double temple in Egypt: the southern hall is dedicated to the crocodile god Sobek, and the northern hall to the falcon god Horus. The temple's architecture is built along a central axis, dividing it into two perfectly symmetrical halves, north and south, each with its own entrance, courtyard, hypostyle hall, and inner sanctuary altar. The relief carvings on its stone walls and columns are finely detailed, with lifelike figural decoration, and also include images such as a solar calendar, medical and surgical instruments, and a woman giving birth in a seated position. The crocodile museum inside the temple houses numerous crocodile mummies.

notes.Obidos 是葡萄牙古城，位於首都里斯本北方約九十公里。紀元前三百年就有腓尼基:
Obidos is an ancient Portuguese town located about ninety kilometers north of the capital, Lisbon. Phoenicians already lived here three hundred years before the Common Era, and more than two thousand years ago the Romans built fortifications and settlements here. In the early eighth century, Moors from North Africa occupied most of Spain and Portugal and built a castle and walls at Obidos. It was not until 1148 that the first king of the Kingdom of Portugal drove out the Moors, ending more than four hundred years of Muslim rule. In 1228, Queen Dona Isabel visited the ancient town of Obidos and fell in love with it at first sight; King Diniz I, to express his affection, gave her the town as a wedding gift, and from then on it was known as the 'Queen's Castle.' In 1441, the ten-year-old King Afonso V married his eight-year-old cousin, Princess Isabella of Coimbra, in a wedding held at the Church of Santa Maria, giving Obidos the further name 'City of the White Wedding.' This ancient town has been voted one of the world's ten most romantic wedding destinations.
Obidos sits on the Atlantic coast, an ancient town lost in time, a tranquil world enclosed by stone walls, known as the 'Pearl in the Valley.' The small town within its tall walls is set apart from the noise and bustle of everyday life, giving off an old medieval air and a fairy-tale-like purity and enchantment. Its cobblestone lanes wind and intertwine, with winding paths and low walls dotted with flowers. The houses on either side, arranged with pleasing irregularity, combine white walls and red roof tiles with sea-like blue and earthy ochre to form the town's dominant palette, lending a sense of natural, simple, unhurried ease and pleasure. Wandering through at will, one takes in the ingenious little craft shops, the colorful arrangements on the walls, the elegant street lamps, and the fragrance of chocolate and strawberry liqueur, all evoking a quiet, detached contentment. The alleys are secluded and enduring, with poetry and beauty quietly appearing at every turn. The white walls and bell tower of the Church of Santa Maria, with their Baroque ornamentation, exude classical grace and refinement. The old town's terrain rises and falls, its winding paths like a beautiful melody extending up into the hills and along the town walls. Climbing the walls and looking out in every direction, on one side rows of red-tiled roofs stretch out with vineyards fading into a hazy green horizon, while on the other side the town walls curve away in parallel lines, disappearing into misty rain as quietly as a page from history. Wandering back and forth here, one feels, without quite noticing it, the contented ease of 'walking to where the water ends, then sitting to watch the clouds rise.'

Both the micrometer (um) and the nanometer (nm) are units of measurement. "Nano" comes from the Greek word for dwarf. A nanometer is one billionth of a meter, or one fifty-thousandth the thickness of a human hair. Scientists refer to the realm larger than 100 nanometers as the macroscopic world, the realm from 1 to 100 nanometers as the mesoscopic world, and anything smaller than 1 nanometer as the microscopic world. At present, humans are already able to observe and manipulate the mesoscopic realm. As for certain structures in the microscopic world, models can only be built through indirect evidence; American physicist Richard Feynman said: "There is plenty of room at the bottom." The nano world is boundlessly vast, and what makes it so fascinating is that within this scale there are many special physical and chemical effects — once matter is "nano-sized," its physical properties such as sound, optical, electrical, magnetic, thermal, and mechanical properties all change accordingly. Through the special properties and functions brought about by "nano-sizing," scientists have developed a very broad range of "nanotechnology." Fields such as biology, the environment, materials, medicine, transportation, and food have all benefited from advances in nanotechnology, gaining new directions and remarkable results. Moreover, precision machinery, artificial intelligence, and even industry in general have advanced rapidly because of this, entering an entirely new phase.

Ansel Adams (1902-1984) was born in San Francisco, USA. He was an outstanding landscape photographer, photography educator and writer, a conservationist, and the originator of the "Zone System" of exposure. He was renowned for his black-and-white landscape works, most famously his series on Yosemite National Park. Throughout his life he was devoted to using photographic craft to reveal the magnificent beauty of nature, "completely abandoning photography's documentary function, making photography a purely technical operation and a tool for the expression of beauty." Adams used "pure" photographic art to portray the real and beautiful world, awakening photographers' attention to the expressive qualities and boundless potential of pure photographic art. Adams believed that photographers, like other artists, choose subjects and fields uniquely their own through which to express the world and themselves. Over more than sixty years of photographic creation, he remained renowned worldwide for his landscape photography. His works, through masterful and flawless photographic form, presented moving scenery, interpreting nature through his personal vision, and made people aware of the importance of protecting the natural environment. In 1980 he received the United States "Presidential Medal of Freedom."
"At one with the power of the American landscape, and renowned for the patient skill and timeless beauty of his work, photographer Ansel Adams has been a visionary in his efforts to preserve this country's wild and scenic areas, both on film and on Earth. Drawn to the beauty of nature's monuments, he is regarded by environmentalists as a monument himself, and by photographers as a national institution. It is through his foresight and fortitude that so much of America has been saved for future Americans."      President James E. The Butterfly Effect refers to the phenomenon whereby, within a dynamic system, a minute change in initial conditions can set off a long-term, enormous chain reaction throughout the entire system. This is a form of chaotic phenomenon. In the development of anything there exist both fixed factors and variables; the trajectory of development follows certain discernible patterns, yet there also exist unpredictable "variables," which often produce results contrary to expectation — showing that the development of things is inherently complex. The most common illustration of this effect is: "A butterfly in the Amazon rainforest of South America flaps its wings a few times, and this can, two weeks later, trigger a tornado in Texas, USA." The reason is that the motion of the butterfly's wing-flapping causes changes in the air system around it, producing a faint air current; this faint air current in turn causes corresponding changes in the surrounding air or other systems, thereby triggering a chain reaction that ultimately leads to enormous changes in other systems.

Xi Murong (1943- ), whose original name is Mulun Xilianbo, is a contemporary painter, poet, and essayist. She graduated from the Fine Arts Department of Taiwan Provincial Normal University in 1963, and from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Brussels, Belgium in 1966, where she received the Belgian Royal Gold Medal and other awards. She has authored more than fifty collections of poetry, essays, art books, and anthologies. Her early works are noted for their fluent language, elegant style, and lyrical rhythm, creating a beautiful, dreamlike mood. Xi Murong's works mostly write of love, life, and homesickness, with elegant, clear phrasing and lively lyricism, brimming with sincere devotion to life; she influenced an entire generation growing up in Taiwan. In 1984, six of her works including 《Seven-Mile Fragrance》 and 《Youth Without Regret》 simultaneously ranked among the top ten bestsellers, earning that year the reputation of "the Year of Xi Murong." In 2014 she received Taiwan's "Annual Poetry Award." In recent years, as the years have passed, her poetic style has shifted to become more measured and cool, especially in the poems on the theme of her homeland, Mongolia, which move between Mongolian history and culture, with a poetic vision that is vast and expansive, carrying the beauty of the desolate, deep, and open grandeur of the frontier. Her 2011 poetry collection 《In the Name of Poetry》 includes many epic poems steeped in the spirit of the grasslands. In 2017 she published 《When the Summer Night Is Fragrant: Selected Paintings of Xi Murong》, presenting herself through poetry and painting.

Tyzen Hsiao (1938-2015) was born in Fengshan, Kaohsiung. He began receiving music instruction from his mother at age five, and from childhood was immersed in church music and Western classical music. He successively graduated from the Music Program of Taiwan Provincial Normal College (now the Department of Music of National Taiwan Normal University), the Keyboard Program of Musashino Academia Musicae in Japan, and the Graduate School of Music at California State University, Los Angeles. He was at once a teacher, pianist, conductor, and composer. In his compositions, he took "the spirit of Taiwanese folk songs as the core, blending in the techniques of Western classical, romantic, impressionist, and modern music, to cultivate a modern new Taiwanese music." He was praised as "Taiwan's Rachmaninoff — the last Romantic poet of the piano." Tyzen Hsiao's works are quite diverse; below are some of his major works.
Concertos: "Violin Concerto in D Major," "Cello Concerto in C Major, Op. 52," "Piano Concerto in C Minor, Op. 53"
Orchestral works: "1947 Overture," "Formosa Symphony," "Angel from Formosa"
Chamber music: "Taiwan Aboriginal Suite," "Piano Trio 'Formosa'"
Choral works: "Ode to Jade Mountain," "Green Taiwan," "Ah! Formosa — Requiem for the Martyrs"
Instrumental works: Ode to Taiwan, Meditation, Harvest (piano four-hands)
Tyzen Hsiao came from a family of cultural refinement, yet his life was filled with hardship and displacement, and he suffered a great deal from illness. However, through steadfast faith and love for the land of Taiwan, he never yielded to circumstance, but continually surpassed himself, burning his life into countless sacred works in praise of God and works expressing concern for Taiwan; as a result, his works are especially moving, needing no explanation in words — one is naturally moved by his music. He won Taiwan's Golden Melody Award three times (2004, 2010, 2011); the 2011 Golden Melody Award was the "Special Contribution Award" in the traditional and art music category.
《The One Away From Home》 was composed in 1978 in Atlanta, a song deeply beloved by overseas compatriots, fully expressing the feelings of those far from home and their longing that remains tied to their native land. The composer later arranged his original solo piece into a choral work. Owing to the beautiful and moving imagery of its lyrics and melody, whether performed as a solo, choral piece, or instrumental piece, it stirs the sentiments of those who have left their hometown, and their longing for their native land.

"April Rain Violin Fantasy Concerto," arranged by Li Che-yi
This concerto draws on three famous songs by Deng Yu-hsien, the father of Taiwanese folk song: "Four Seasons Red," "Moonlit Night Sorrow," and "Flower in the Rainy Night." Built on the melodies of these three well-known songs, it goes beyond the richness achieved by orchestrating folk tunes symphonically; through the interplay of the violin's melodic lines with the orchestra's rhythm, it adds a modern sensibility and coloristic variation to these classic songs.
The first New Year's concert devoted specifically to Taiwan was held in Taipei on January 1, 2019. Violin virtuoso Tseng Keng-yuan returned specially from the United States to take part, performing this "April Rain Violin Fantasy Concerto" with the Formosa Chamber Orchestra under conductor Li Che-yi.
Violinist Tseng Keng-yuan. In 1983 the violin master Henryk Szeryng predicted that Tseng Keng-yuan would "become a violin master of the twenty-first century." Tseng began studying violin at age five under the guidance of his father, Tseng Che-nan, and gave his first public performance at age six. In 1978 Tseng met Erick Friedman, a direct disciple of Jascha Heifetz, who called him a talent seen only once in twelve years. With Friedman's help, Tseng won a full scholarship to the Manhattan School of Music and studied under him. While in the United States, Tseng won prizes in numerous competitions, and in 1988 performed twice at the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. In 1990 he took part in the Tchaikovsky International Competition in Moscow and won the award for best interpretation of a new work; some veteran music lovers remarked that it was "as if seeing Heifetz himself again." At the 1993 Queen Elisabeth International Music Competition in Belgium, he won the silver medal, having received the highest scores in the first round, and was immediately received by the Queen. He was hailed as the greatest Eastern performer in history and given the title "Magician of the Bow." Tseng Keng-yuan currently teaches at the Peabody Institute of the Johns Hopkins University, where he also serves as chair of the string department; he is a visiting director at the Yong Siew Toh Conservatory of Music at the National University of Singapore, and artistic director of Taiwan's Xuanyin International Music Festival.
-- (Excerpted from Dr. Lin Heng-che's blog post, "Heifetz's Successor in Taiwan -- Violinist Tseng Keng-yuan," August 30, 2015.)

The melody of "Longing for Home, Going Home" comes from the Largo, the second movement of the "Ninth Symphony" (also known as the "New World Symphony") by the Czech composer Antonin Leopold Dvorak (1841-1904). The movement faintly echoes the melodies of African American spirituals from the American South. In 1969, when humans first landed on the moon, astronaut Neil Armstrong carried with him a recording of the "New World Symphony."

Li Tai-hsiang (1941-2014) was a member of the Amis Indigenous people from Malan Township in Taitung, Taiwan. He graduated from the music department of the National Taiwan Academy of Arts and later served as concertmaster of the Taipei Symphony Orchestra and as conductor of the Taiwan Provincial Symphony Orchestra, among other posts. In 1973 he received a Rockefeller Foundation scholarship from the United States and, at the invitation of the U.S. State Department, traveled to the United States to study further at the Center for Music Experiment in San Diego, California.
His musical output spans classical, experimental, and popular genres. After 1976 he devoted himself to promoting folk music, opening new space between art music and popular music, and creating many widely sung works of "popular art song," including "The Olive Tree" (lyrics by Sanmao), "Mistake" (lyrics by Cheng Chou-yu), and "Walking in the Rain" (lyrics by Li Tai-hsiang himself). He won Taiwan's Golden Horse Award and Golden Tripod Award. In 1988 he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease but continued to compose local folk songs and orchestral works. In 1997 he received a special Golden Melody Award and the Wu San-lien Award for the Arts. In 2008 he received the Taiwan Literature and Arts Award, the highest cultural honor in Taiwan. In 2013 he received the 32nd Executive Yuan Culture Award. With his solid academy training, lofty musical vision, and abundant romantic sensibility, Li Tai-hsiang was a composer who wove contemporary literature into music, refined Taiwan's popular songs, and brought classical and popular music together. His work drew people from every walk of life, blended different cultures, enriched the campus folk-song movement, and became a clear and powerful current within Taiwanese popular music. His music also helped launch the careers of several celebrated singers who went on to dominate the Taiwanese music scene. In his later years he devoted himself to exploring the powerful Indigenous life force within him, creating the sweeping Amis epic "The Hunt."
notes.《 歸去來兮 》 魏晉。陶淵明\n歸去來兮，田園將蕪，胡不歸！既自以心為形役，:
"The Return" (Gui Qu Lai Xi Ci), Wei-Jin period, by Tao Yuanming
Return home! My fields and garden will soon run wild -- why not go back? Since I have long let my mind be servant to my body, why should I grieve and lament alone? I understand that what is past cannot be corrected, but I know that what is to come can still be pursued. Indeed I have not strayed far from the right path; I realize that today I am right and yesterday I was wrong. My boat rocks gently onward, the wind blows softly and stirs my robes. I ask a traveler about the road ahead, and regret only that the morning light is still so dim. Then I see my modest gate and roof, and I rush forward joyfully. The servants come out to welcome me, my young children wait at the door. The three paths in my garden have gone to weeds, but the pines and chrysanthemums still remain. I lead the children by the hand into the house, where the wine jars are full. I pour myself cup after cup, and gazing at the trees in the courtyard my face relaxes into contentment. I lean against the south window and let my thoughts roam free, realizing how easily one is at peace in a home just big enough to hold one's knees. Each day I stroll through the garden and find delight in it; though there is a gate, it stays shut most of the time. Leaning on my staff I wander and rest, and from time to time I raise my head to gaze into the distance. Clouds drift aimlessly out from the mountain peaks; birds, weary of flying, know when to return to their nests. As the sunlight dims and is about to fade, I stroke a solitary pine and linger there.

"Night Rain in the Harbor City" is a Taiwanese-language popular song from the postwar era, with lyrics by Lu Chuan-tzu and music by Yang San-lang, published in 1958. The melody was originally composed by Yang San-lang without any lyrics. In the early 1950s, Yang San-lang worked in Keelung as bandleader -- and also as a trumpet player -- for the "International Friendship Club" that entertained U.S. troops stationed in Taiwan. Keelung has rain nearly every day, and in 1951 Yang was suddenly inspired while in the rain; using the natural minor and harmonic minor scales, he played a mournful melody on his trumpet called "Rain Blues." He played it every day and it was well liked by the American servicemen, but for a long time it had no lyrics. One day, Lu Chuan-tzu, a musician in the band, was moved to write lyrics evoking the sorrowful image of a man who drifts from harbor city to harbor city, making his home everywhere, watching the night rain. He gave the lyrics to Wang Yun-feng, composer of "Mending the Broken Net," to refine, and the song became a well-known number at the International Friendship Club. In 1958 Yang San-lang gave the song to Wu Chin-huai to record and publish. Later, a Christian group set new lyrics to the melody and adapted it into a hymn.
-- (Excerpted from Wikipedia)

Chen Hsiu-hsi (1921-1991), a native of Hsinchu, Taiwan, who lived for many years in Guanziling, Chiayi, in a home called "Li Yuan," was known as "Taiwan's remarkable woman," "Taiwan's first female poet," and "a pioneer of Taiwanese feminist poetry." The 1970s were a period when young poetry societies rose up in Taiwan. After publishing her first Chinese-language poetry collection, "Overturned Leaves," in 1971, Chen Hsiu-hsi became active in the modern poetry scene and served as president of the Li Poetry Society for twenty years (1971-1991), a period during which the Li poetry journal grew and flourished, and one that also coincided with a flourishing of Taiwanese consciousness, democracy, and social movements. After the 1977 Nativist Literature Debate, Chen Hsiu-hsi's 1973 poem "Taiwan" was adapted by Professor Liang Ching-feng, retitled "Formosa," and set to music by Li Shuang-tse; folk singers such as Hu Te-fu and Yang Tsu-chun performed it, and it swept through campuses and was sung across the entire island. The poem's language fits Taiwan closely, its tone gentle and understated, expressing the feelings of the Taiwanese people. It was banned from performance during martial law for as long as eight years. Through her role as an active and gentle presence among poets, her tender and compassionate poetic style, and her example as an elder, Chen Hsiu-hsi won the shared affection of the poetry world. Her poems are full of care and hope, and her poetic spirit continues to be sung across the island. (Min Pao, September 2, 2015)

Song Tse-lai's poem "If You Come to Hengchun" was written in 1981 and is an important work of the early Taiwanese-language literature movement. It has been widely recited, partly because of its rhyme scheme: apart from the fifteenth line, the entire poem keeps a single rhyme throughout, with every line rhyming, so that reciting it feels like singing a folk song. Reading it aloud in Taiwanese brings out the beauty of its sound even more, echoing the beautiful scenery of Hengchun. Song Tse-lai's major works include the novel series "Dahuinan Village" and "Ruins of Taiwan"; the essay collections "Ten Nights of Talk on Literature" and "Seven Letters to the Taiwanese Literary World"; the poetry collection "Ode to Formosa"; and he founded magazines such as "Taiwan New Culture," "Taiwan New Literature," and "Taiwan E Literature and Art."
Chen Ta (1906-1981), a native of Hengchun, Pingtung, Taiwan, was a folk singer regarded as a national treasure. He was known for performances that combined playing the moon lute (yueqin) with storytelling in a distinctive personal style. His singing voice was desolate and moving, his lyrics had a poetic quality, and combined with the unaccompanied melodies of the moon lute and his abundant emotion, he was widely beloved; his most famous song was "Thoughts Arise" (Su-siong-khi).
The "mountain-descending wind" (luoshanfeng) is a weather phenomenon unique to the Hengchun Peninsula. It occurs because, from October through April of the following year, the northeast monsoon flows from north to south along the 3,000-meter peaks of the Central Mountain Range; the range grows progressively lower toward the south, and by the time it reaches the Dawu Mountain area of the Hengchun Peninsula, its height has dropped to below 1,000 to 400 meters. This produces a powerful downslope wind pouring over the mountains, known as the "mountain-descending wind." Its instantaneous intensity can reach force 6 or 7, comparable to a mild typhoon, and it can sometimes last for several days.

"The Blue Danube" is a waltz composed in 1867 by the Austrian composer Johann Strauss II. Together with "Tales from the Vienna Woods" and the "Emperor Waltz," it is counted among Strauss's three great waltzes; of these, "The Blue Danube" is the most celebrated and has become synonymous with the Viennese waltz. It achieved enormous success at the 1867 Paris World's Fair and has since been performed around the world. It is now regarded as Austria's "second national anthem" and is one of the pieces traditionally always performed at the Vienna New Year's Concert.
Johann Strauss composed "The Blue Danube Waltz" after the Austrian Empire's crushing defeat in the Austro-Prussian War, to help the public shake off their gloom and depression -- a waltz symbolizing "the vitality of Vienna's life." After hearing this familiar and moving melody, do you feel hope and vitality stirring within you? Do you seem to see the swaying willows along the banks of the Danube, the smoke rising from village hearths at the far edge of the fields, the distant mountains wrapped in swirling mist, and the hazy pale blue color of the river's surface...

notes.《Annie Laurie》（安娜羅荔）是一首膾炙人口的蘇格蘭民歌，旋律優美哀婉: "Annie Laurie" is a beloved and widely sung Scottish folk song, with a beautiful, mournful melody and lyrics full of deep feeling. Behind this song lies a moving love story connected to a Scottish noblewoman of the 17th century. Annie Laurie was a real historical figure from the Dumfries region of southern Scotland. She was born in 1682, the daughter of Maxwell of Craigieburn. According to legend, in her youth she fell in love with a young officer named William Douglas of Fingland, but because of the difference in their social standing, Annie's father opposed the match, and the two were ultimately unable to marry. Heartbroken, William Douglas put his love for Annie into a poem, the first version of which appeared around 1700. This poem later became the core lyrics of the song. The earliest version of the poem had only a few stanzas and was written in a somewhat archaic style of English. Later, in the mid-19th century, the Scottish poet Alicia Scott (1810-1900) rewrote the lyrics to make them gentler and more accessible to a popular audience, and set them to a melody (possibly adapted from a traditional tune), producing the version familiar to us today.
notes.《Loch Lomond》 ( 羅莽湖畔 ) 是一首傳唱久遠的蘇格蘭民謠，浸染着: "Loch Lomond" is a long-cherished Scottish folk song steeped in a tragic chapter of Scottish history. In 1745, the Jacobites, made up mainly of Scottish Highland clans, launched their second large-scale uprising against the government in London. After several battles, the Scottish forces at one point advanced as far as Derby, only about 130 miles from London, shaking the capital. But in April of the following year, 1746, the Jacobites were decisively crushed at the Battle of Culloden in Scotland, bringing to an end the Jacobite rebellion that had lasted more than half a century. In this battle, the British army imprisoned captured Scots in Carlisle Castle, near the Scottish border. The English applied no fixed standard in dealing with these Scottish prisoners, choosing at random -- some were executed, others released. It is said that one of the Scottish prisoners, sensing that he was about to be executed, wrote the song "Loch Lomond" and entrusted it to a fellow prisoner who was being released, asking him to carry it back to his beloved, who lived by the banks of Loch Lomond. This sorrowful, plaintive ballad has drifted ever since across the hills and moors of Scotland, carried on through the mist, sung continuously down to the present day.
notes.《My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean》 ( 我的邦妮 ): "My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean" is a song in the Scottish folk style, with a smooth, catchy melody. It is widely sung, but the story behind its origin carries elements of history and legend. The most widely known account holds that the song is connected to Charles Edward Stuart, the 18th-century claimant to the Scottish throne, nicknamed "Bonnie Prince Charlie." In 1745, Prince Charles launched the Jacobite Rebellion, attempting to restore his father's Stuart line to the thrones of England and Scotland. After his defeat at the Battle of Culloden in 1746, Charles fled into exile in France and never returned to Scotland. Some believe the song expresses the Scottish people's longing for him after he left "across the ocean," and their hope for his return. Although this account is not confirmed by any direct historical documentation, since "Bonnie" means "beautiful" or "handsome" in Scots and matches Prince Charles's nickname, this interpretation has been widely accepted.

"Winterreise" (Winter Journey) was composed by the Austrian musician Franz Schubert (1797-1828), based on the poem cycle of the same name by the German Romantic poet Wilhelm Müller. It is a representative work among Schubert's art songs. "Winterreise" is a vocal cycle made up of 24 songs strung together. It is a lyrical musical poem, a musical drama. Through melody and timbre, Schubert deliberately depicted the inner world of the protagonist, portraying the lonely, wandering, isolated soul described in Müller's poems—dissatisfied with reality, single-mindedly pursuing a distant and illusory ideal world, yet never able to attain it, an anguished spirit. "Der Lindenbaum" (The Linden Tree) is the fifth of the 24 songs in "Winterreise." When Schubert composed "Winterreise," he was physically weak and felt deeply lonely, so the mood of this song cycle is quite somber—especially this song, "Der Lindenbaum," whose lyrics and melody describe the wanderer drifting between memory, hope, regret, and helplessness. "Der Lindenbaum" is one of Schubert's most famous songs; its folk-song quality has spread across the world and through the generations. Schubert died the year after completing "Winterreise," at only 31 years old. In his short life, this most poetic of musicians composed more than 600 songs—including "Heidenröslein" (Wild Rose), "Die Forelle" (The Trout), and "Die schöne Müllerin" (The Fair Maid of the Mill)—as well as 18 operas and 9 symphonies, including the famous "Unfinished Symphony."

Passing through the darkness, I could see nothing clearly
I seemed to faintly hear it rustling above, speaking to me
"Friend, come to me here, and you will find peace"
In fact, the original German title of this song, "Der Lindenbaum," should be translated as "linden tree," but in 1909 the Japanese translator Kondō Sakufū had already rendered it as "Bodhi tree," and the Chinese translation has followed this ever since—a beautiful mistake, as it were.

notes.《唐吉訶德》 ( Don Quixote ) 是西班牙作家塞萬提斯的作品 (: "Don Quixote" (Don Quixote) is a work by the Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes (1615), regarded as a paragon of Spanish literature and one of the foundational works of modern Western literature. The protagonist, Don Quixote, is a gaunt, declined nobleman who, wearing a helmet with a hole in it, wielding a rusted lance, and riding an exhausted, skinny horse, travels the world together with his servant Sancho, righting wrongs wherever he goes. His whole experience unfolds between fantasy and reality, between good intentions and blind action—a figure who embodies contradiction in one body, at once comic and tragic. notes.《夜晚露天咖啡座》(The Café Terrace on the Place: "The Café Terrace on the Place du Forum" (The Café Terrace on the Place du Forum) is one of Van Gogh's famous works. This is Van Gogh's first painting with a starry-sky background; his other paintings with starry backgrounds include "Starry Night Over the Rhône" and "The Starry Night." This painting displays Van Gogh's distinctive warm color tones and use of perspective. The glow of the yellow café and the deep blue of the starry sky form an interesting contrast; the sky, the stars, the lights, and the human figures play off one another, making the night's atmosphere all the more mysterious and enchanting. Van Gogh sought, through emotive brushwork and rich color, to express his subjective feelings and inner experience, conveying his inner loneliness and his longing for human companionship. The whole painting radiates a soft, poetic quality while also brewing a rising vitality.
notes.《日出 · 印象》（Impression Sunrise）是法國印象派畫家克勞德: "Impression, Sunrise" (Impression Sunrise) is an oil painting created in 1872 by the French Impressionist painter Claude Monet. The painting depicts a sunrise over a harbor shrouded in morning mist, using the marvelous shifting and shimmering of light and quick, leaping brushstrokes to convey the fascinating way light reflects and trembles on the surface of the sea. This work broke through the framework of traditional subject matter and composition, taking visual perception as its point of departure and emphasizing the atmosphere created by changes in light. It is the most typical of Monet's paintings, a classic work of Impressionism, and the very origin of the name "Impressionism."

"The Olive Tree" is one of the most representative lyrical songs in the Chinese-speaking world, with lyrics by Sanmao and music by Li Tai-hsiang. The song opens with the repeated, questioning refrain "Don't ask me where I come from / my hometown is far away," then immediately raises the central question of "why wander," turning the departure of an individual life into a spiritual and soulful journey. The "olive tree" in the song is not a specific geographic place, but a symbol of ideals, faith, and an inner resting place—a goal sought while walking, held onto in solitude. The melody is simple yet far-reaching, almost chant-like, carrying a faint homesickness together with an unyielding will toward freedom; the wording is spare yet resonates in layer upon layer, transforming the wanderer's loneliness into a force of self-affirmation. For this reason, "The Olive Tree" is not merely a song of homesickness, but a song about "why we go on"—even if the road ahead is long and the destination unclear, one must follow the olive tree in one's heart and keep walking.

notes.《老人與海》是海明威創作生涯的代表作品，是世界小說創作的經典。海明威於1954獲: "The Old Man and the Sea" is the representative work of Hemingway's writing career and a classic of world fiction. Hemingway won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954. The theme of "The Old Man and the Sea" is similar to that of Melville's "Moby-Dick": both depict the struggle and striving between man and nature. "Moby-Dick" tells the story of Captain Ahab, who single-mindedly pursues and hunts the great white whale; because this violates the laws of nature, and because of his arbitrary, self-willed obsession—even wagering his life and his very humanity against fate—he ultimately pays with his life, swallowed by the sea. In contrast, the old fisherman of "The Old Man and the Sea," while struggling against nature, remains calm and steady in spirit, following the way of heaven and the seasons. While displaying such noble human qualities as perseverance, courage, faith, and determination, he comes to understand the way in which all things live and coexist, and thereby becomes one with the essential nature and the workings of the natural world. "The Old Man and the Sea" points toward a certain state of human existence, and carries symbolic meaning that reminds us of the many dimensions of life.
notes.《追憶似水年華》是法國作家馬塞爾·普魯斯特（1871年—1922年）的作品，以其: "In Search of Lost Time" is a work by the French writer Marcel Proust (1871-1922), renowned for its length and its stream-of-consciousness technique. This work portrays with great subtlety the French upper class and literary circles of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, shifting from a straightforward depiction of human society toward an analysis of human psychology and emotion, thereby achieving the first mature dissection of human feeling in a literary work and opening the way for the "stream of consciousness" novel—becoming a landmark of a new literary form in literary history. The overall structure of the work is the narrator's retrospective review of past experiences he has lived through, and this act of retrospection is itself a struggle against forgetting. At the same time, this work is the first to take the birth of a work itself as its subject matter; Proust believed that human life becomes "true life" only in memory, that "life as recalled in memory is more real than the reality lived at that time and place." André Maurois notes in his preface: "The only true paradise is the paradise we have lost," and "the happy years are the lost years." (Excerpted from Wikipedia)

"Visiting a Hermit and Not Finding Him": "Beneath the pine I asked the boy; he said his master had gone to gather herbs. He is somewhere within these mountains, but the clouds are deep and I do not know where" is the representative work of the Tang-dynasty poet Jia Dao (779-840). Jia Dao was a poet of the "painstaking chanting" school; the famous story of "tui qiao" ("push or knock") originates with him. Legend has it that, riding on his donkey, he pondered deeply over the two lines "The birds roost in the trees by the pond; a monk knocks at the gate beneath the moon," repeatedly weighing whether to use "push" or "knock," so absorbed that he wandered by mistake into Han Yu's honor-guard procession. Han Yu suggested using "knock," since the word produces a sound, and in the depths of night this adds a rhythm of motion within stillness. Jia Dao himself said of these two lines, "Two lines took three years to complete; a single recitation brings tears to both eyes." Later, people came to call the process of deliberating over word choice "tui qiao."
Jia Dao's "Visiting a Hermit and Not Finding Him" uses the most common materials of reclusion poetry—namely, pines and clouds—and through the pine, the clouds, and the boy, it creates the hazy, elusive Chan (Zen) mood and contemplation of "one question, three answers, and yet no resolution." This poem also embodies the technique of "spatial expansion" found in classical Chinese poetry—that is, the visual scope of the poem widens from near to far, from small to large, so that the field of view grows ever wider, finally entering into a vast, boundless realm. The "beneath the pine" of the first line is a localized point of origin; the "gone to gather herbs" of the second line extends from beneath the pine onto the road of gathering herbs, a linear extension; the "in the mountains" of the third line is a plane, a further layer; and the "the clouds are deep, I do not know where" of the fourth line is the infinite expansion of that plane. The whole poem expands from point to line to plane, growing broader and broader until it reaches a vast expanse, achieving the flavor of "words that end, yet meaning that never ends."

notes.「壓垮駱駝的最後一根稻草，The last straw that breaks: The familiar saying "the last straw that breaks a camel's back" comes from an Arabic fable. A farmer wanted to test how much weight the camel he kept could bear, so he kept piling straw onto its back, until the final piece of straw caused the camel to collapse. This shows that the camel collapsed because too much pressure had accumulated without being noticed and stopped in time. Although that final straw is critical, it is often not the true cause.
notes.「大漠孤烟直，長河落日圓」, 是唐朝詩人王維《使至塞上》詩中的千古名句。這两句詩: "In the vast desert, a lone plume of smoke rises straight; over the long river, the setting sun is round" is an enduringly famous line from the Tang dynasty poet Wang Wei's poem "Sent to the Frontier." These two lines fully embody the quality of "painting within poetry" that characterizes Wang Wei's work, with a vivid, picture-like sense of scene. First, the composition is picture-like: from the setting sun on the horizon, to the beacon smoke in the sky, down to the river on the ground -- smoke nearby, the sunset in the distance, and the boundless desert as backdrop. In just a few words, the layers are arranged with clarity, sketching out an almost abstract painterly mood. Second, the lines are as carefully composed as in a painting: across the boundless desert, lines crisscross vertically and horizontally -- the vertical line is the rising wisp of smoke, the horizontal line is the leisurely flowing river, and the circle is the slowly setting sun. Third, the colors are rich: the vast rolling sand is the mighty desert, the orange-red is the floating sunset, the shimmering white silk is the distant river, and the deepening blue-grey haze is the solitary column of grey smoke. Su Dongpo's comment on Wang Wei -- "Savor Mojie's poetry, and there is painting within the poetry; savor Mojie's paintings, and there is poetry within the painting" -- is indeed most fitting.

notes.「小確幸」 一詞源自村上春樹的隨筆集《蘭格漢斯島的午后》。二十五篇散文寫的都是生: The term "xiao que xing" (a small but certain happiness) originates from Haruki Murakami's essay collection "Afternoon in the Islands of Langerhans." Its twenty-five essays all describe everyday trivialities; unlike his novels, his essays are plain and unadorned, free of melancholy or loneliness, and through a keen, distinctive perspective, ordinary people and events appear light, meaningful, humorous, and endearing. One of the essays is titled "A Small Certain Happiness," referring to "a small but definite happiness and satisfaction" in daily life. Through translator Lin Shaohua's literal rendering, the term became a widely used colloquial expression across the Chinese-speaking world. In everyday life there flow certain fleeting moments of happiness and beauty -- whether inner contentment and ease of mind, or gratitude and appreciation for life. When we gather up these small certain happinesses one by one, they become life's simplest moments of joy.

notes.「油菜花籽命」，是指早時女人的命運就像油菜花籽一般，隨風而定，隨運而生，飄到那裡: "The fate of rapeseed" refers to the idea that, in earlier times, a woman's fate was like a rapeseed: determined by the wind, arising by chance, taking root wherever it happened to land. It carries the meaning of "marry a rooster, follow the rooster; marry a dog, follow the dog" -- submitting to fate and yielding to circumstance. Rapeseed (rape flower, rapeseed flower), also called caizi or youcaizi, is a plant of the mustard family, tolerant of cold, drought, salt, and dampness, with strong adaptability to its environment. For this reason, "the fate of the rapeseed" is also used to describe hardworking, resilient women, signifying a woman's tenacious strength in adapting to her surroundings and putting down roots wherever she lands. Liao Huiying's celebrated novel "Oil-Hemp Rapeseed" (1982) offers a profound account of "a woman's rapeseed fate." The novel has been praised as capturing in a single stroke thirty years of the bitter lives of Taiwanese women, standing as a precious record of Taiwanese women's coming of age, a pioneering work of the feminist movement that ushered in an era of women's self-awareness and influenced women's choices to break free from traditional fate.

Suddenly he awoke, and there he was, unmistakably Zhuang Zhou. He did not know whether it was Zhuang Zhou who had dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming that it was Zhuang Zhou. Between Zhuang Zhou and the butterfly there must be some distinction -- this is called the transformation of things." Zhuangzi used this story to illustrate the idea that things and self are one, and that the ten thousand things are equal. Zhuangzi, given name Zhou, courtesy name Zixiu, was born around 369 BCE, a native of the state of Song during the Warring States period. He was a renowned thinker, philosopher, and man of letters, a representative figure of the Daoist school, and the successor and developer of Laozi's philosophical thought -- together known as "Lao-Zhuang philosophy."

notes.一府二鹿三艋舺，是一句台灣諺語，描叙清朝時期全島三大港市的盛況。一府是台南府，二: "First Fu, second Lu, third Mengjia" is a Taiwanese proverb describing the prosperity of the island's three great port cities during the Qing dynasty. "Fu" refers to Tainan Prefecture, "Lu" refers to Lukang Township in Changhua, and "Mengjia" refers to Mengjia in Taipei (present-day Wanhua). The proverb reflects the history of Taiwan's development from south to north, and the reliance of each region on maritime trade. Lukang ("deer port") may have gotten its name because herds of deer gathered there at the time, and deer antlers, hides, and dried venison were exported from the port. Lukang's rise was due to a number of geographic advantages. As a river port city, it had direct access to the Taiwan Strait, and the sea voyage from Lukang to the Fujian-Guangdong coast of mainland China was the shortest among all of Taiwan's ports. At the time, the main channel of the Zhuoshui River flowed out to sea at Lukang, allowing ships to travel upstream and connect with various parts of central Taiwan. The period from 1785 to 1845 was Lukang's golden age. Afterward, Lukang's advantages as a port gradually declined due to silt accumulation, and the once-crowded harbor of a thousand sails lost its former glory. After the middle years of the Jiaqing era, merchant ships shifted to Wanggong Port in the south. During the Daoguang era, Wanggong Port in turn began to silt up.

Vivaldi (Antonio Lucio Vivaldi, 1678-1741) was an Italian born in Venice. Venice, the city of water, is an extremely romantic city full of music. At that time, Italy had already developed into a major center of European Baroque music, and the confluence of favorable timing and place nurtured Vivaldi's great music. The musical genres for which Vivaldi is best remembered by later generations are opera and the concerto; among his many concertos, the most outstanding and best known is the violin concerto set "The Four Seasons." Nearly three hundred years later, this music still sounds fresh today, having completely broken free of the constraints of time and place -- it is a great treasure of human musical art. "The Four Seasons" consists of violin concertos titled No. 1 "Spring," No. 2 "Summer," No. 3 "Autumn," and No. 4 "Winter," each composed of the standard fast-slow-fast three-movement concerto structure. In other words, "The Four Seasons" is actually four independent three-movement violin concertos, but because of the thematic connection (the seasons), they are regarded as a single set of works and collectively called "The Four Seasons." The music is paired with accompanying sonnets, whose content depicts the distinctive scenery of each season.
notes.九份位於新北市瑞芳區，臨近金瓜石和雞籠山，是昔日的採金礦中心。環山面海，擁有多變: Jiufen is located in Ruifang District, New Taipei City, near Jinguashi and Jilong Mountain, and was once a center of gold mining. Surrounded by mountains and facing the sea, it possesses ever-changing mountain and ocean scenery, and is a small mountain town that retains the simple, rustic character of earlier times. According to records in the "Taipei County Gazetteer," in the early Qing dynasty this poor, remote village had only nine households, so whenever people went out to the market to shop or when cargo ships arrived, each of the nine households would need a share -- hence the village came to be called "Jiufen" (literally "nine shares"), a name still in use today. Gold mining in Jiufen and Jinguashi has a history of at least a hundred years. In 1894, a gold vein was discovered in the Jiufen area, and large crowds of gold prospectors and miners poured in, beginning Jiufen's golden age of prosperity. At the height of gold mining, Jiufen once earned the nickname "Little Hong Kong" or "Little Shanghai," and local residents' spending power reportedly even exceeded that of Taipei. It is said that the finest establishments and restaurants in all of Taiwan were concentrated in Jiufen at the time, and Taiwan's first movie theater, Shengping Theater, was also built there -- a glimpse of its former prosperity. After 1956, the gold deposits in the Jiufen area were largely exhausted, and following the decline of the mining industry, Jiufen's glory days became history. The population scattered, streets fell into disrepair, and empty houses spread as decline and desolation set in. It was not until the 1990s, when director Hou Hsiao-hsien and screenwriter Wu Nien-jen filmed "A City of Sadness" and "Dust in the Wind" on location in Jiufen, that Jiufen's distinctive old-style street architecture, hillside stone steps, weathered atmosphere, and mountain-and-sea scenery attracted attention from home and abroad through these films, bringing renewed vitality and energy back to Jiufen. This is a classic example of a declining town being reborn through the influence of film. Jiufen's nostalgic beauty, its cultural heritage, and the added flourish of new-wave humanistic style have created an artistic mountain-town atmosphere that has begun to shine brightly within Taiwan's tourism and leisure industry.

notes.亞德里亞海有數的小島和半島，在夏日陽光的照映下，閃耀迷人。曲折的海岸散落著許多村: The Adriatic Sea's numerous small islands and peninsulas shimmer beautifully under the summer sun. Along the winding coastline are scattered many villages and ancient towns, among which Dubrovnik, at the southern tip of Croatia, is the most dazzling and richly evocative of castle romance. After traveling there, the poet Byron called this ancient city "the pearl dropped on the Adriatic shore." It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. Founded in the 6th century, this ancient city has a dazzling array of historical episodes and cultural ups and downs. Its annals span a thousand years: ruled at various times by the Byzantine Empire, held by the Republic of Venice, invaded by the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and controlled by the Ottoman Empire. Just over twenty years ago, amid the chaos following the collapse of Yugoslavia, between 1991 and 1992, the city suffered fierce attacks from the Yugoslav People's Army of neighboring Serbia, lasting nine months. Cut off from water and electricity, and with supplies and reinforcements exhausted, the old town was nonetheless successfully preserved through the resolute strength of its self-organized citizens. The old town is surrounded by tall, thick walls that enclose its layered history, architectural art, and cultural atmosphere. Climbing onto the walls and walking along the stone paving and steps, one can take in the scenery both inside and outside the town, while the vast Adriatic Sea dotted with sails also stirs the spirit. The red tiles, white walls, blue sky, and turquoise waves, arranged near and far, form a scene of extraordinary color.
notes.亞歷山大 . 佛萊明 ( Alexander Fleming，1881—195: Alexander Fleming (1881-1955), a Scottish biologist and pharmacologist, discovered penicillin in a bacterial culture dish in 1928 -- one of the most important achievements in 20th-century medical history. notes.唐朝詩人李白的詩《下終南山過斛斯山人宿置酒》: 「暮從碧山下，山月隨人歸。卻顧所: The Tang Dynasty poet Li Bai's poem "Coming Down from Zhongnan Mountain, Stopping at Hermit Husi's Place for the Night, and Drinking Wine" (下終南山過斛斯山人宿置酒): "At dusk I came down from the green mountain, the mountain moon following me home. Looking back at the path I had come, all was blue-green, crossed by kingfisher-hued mists. Hand in hand we reached the farmer's home, the child opened the bramble gate. Green bamboo led into the secluded path, blue vines brushed my traveling clothes. Happily talking, we found a place to rest, and shared fine wine together. We sang long songs to the wind in the pines, and by the time the tune ended the river of stars had grown sparse. I was drunk and you were happy again — together we forgot all worldly cares in blissful ease." This pastoral poem by Li Bai, on the themes of farm life and drinking wine, was clearly influenced by Tao Yuanming. Tao Yuanming was the originator of pastoral poetry, but his poems were plain and tranquil, as in lines such as "Dimly seen, the distant village; faintly rising, the smoke over the hamlet," "Picking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge, I gaze leisurely at the southern mountain," and "The path is narrow, the grass and trees grow long, the evening dew wets my clothes." Tao Yuanming did not deliberately embellish his language, and his tone was calm, like that of a recluse living at ease, whereas Li Bai freely embellishes his verse with bright colors and lively spirit — singing heartily and reveling in drink with deep feeling — showing how different Li Bai's poetic style was from Tao Yuanming's.

notes.啟示錄 (Book of Revelation，Revelation of Jo:
Revelation (Book of Revelation, Revelation of John): "Revelation" means to bring to light what was originally hidden; it is the final book of the New Testament. This book is a prophetic letter written by the Apostle John to seven churches in Asia Minor. Its central themes concern three major matters: "the things which thou hast seen," "the things which are," and "the things which shall be hereafter." John gives a concrete account of the visions he saw through revelation of the Holy Spirit. Just as Genesis in the Old Testament discusses the origin of all things, Revelation records the culmination of all things. Most of the Old Testament's prophecies find their answer in this book, and the salvation discussed in the New Testament finds its fulfillment here as well. The entire truth of scripture and God's plan of redemption are also expressed and summarized in this book.
John was one of the twelve disciples of Jesus and the author of the Gospel of John in the New Testament. During the extreme persecution of early Christians by the Roman emperors, after Peter and Paul were put to death in one such persecution, John went to Ephesus to serve as overseer of the seven churches of Asia Minor. In 95-96 AD he was exiled by the Roman emperor Domitian (reigned 81-96 AD) to the island of Patmos. During his imprisonment on the island, he recorded the revelations and visions he received. After being released in 96 AD and returning to Ephesus, he completed the writing of Revelation.
Patmos is a small island in the Aegean Sea of Greece, located west of Asia Minor (Turkey), 130 kilometers from Ephesus. It measures roughly 30 by 18 kilometers, a rocky island with rugged terrain. Because of John's story, the island has become a pilgrimage site for believers, earning it the name "Jerusalem of the Aegean." The cave where John was imprisoned is located within the main town of Chora.
notes.嘉南平原是台灣最大的平原，北起虎尾溪，南至鹽水溪，長130公里，寬35公里，包括: The Chianan Plain is Taiwan's largest plain, extending from the Huwei River in the north to the Yanshui River in the south, about 130 kilometers long and 35 kilometers wide, covering Yunlin, Chiayi, and Tainan counties. The whole plain is flat and well-suited for agriculture, but unfortunately most of the rivers crossing the plain were of little use for irrigation. Although rivers such as the Beigang, Bazhang, Jishui, and Zengwen pass through it, they flow swiftly and carry heavy sediment loads; when heavy rains came, sand and gravel would wash down the slopes, silting up the riverbeds and causing floods. In earlier times, farmers suffered greatly from floods, drought, and salt damage, barely managing to harvest sugarcane and coarse grains to survive. To solve the problem of irrigation water for the Chianan Plain, the Japanese colonial government at the time built the Chianan Irrigation Canal and the Wushantou Reservoir. Wushantou Reservoir is Taiwan's largest man-made lake (also called Coral Lake, because its winding shoreline and scattered islands resemble a beautiful green coral reef). It was designed and supervised by Governor-General's Office engineer Hatta Yoichi (1882-1942), begun in 1920, and completed in 1930 after overcoming harsh conditions and rampant disease. Wushantou Reservoir collects water from the upper reaches of the Guantian River, a tributary of the Zengwen River, and is the main water source for the Chianan Irrigation Canal. After leaving Wushantou Reservoir, the water divides into north and south main channels: the north channel crosses the Jishui, Bazhang, and Puzi rivers to reach the south bank of the Beigang River, while the south channel crosses the Guantian River and the Zengwen River to reach Shanhua and connect with branch channels. The Chianan Canal also draws water from the Zhuoshui River, flowing south via the old Huwei River to connect with the north channel. In this way, a spiderweb-like network of waterways was built across the entire Chianan Plain — this is the Chianan Irrigation Canal. Former President Lee Teng-hui often lamented: "Many people don't know just how long the Chianan Canal really is." The main supply channels total 10,000 kilometers in length, and the drainage channels total 6,000 kilometers, for a combined total of 16,000 kilometers — equivalent to half the circumference of the earth. After the completion of the Chianan Canal, irrigated paddy fields on the Chianan Plain increased thirtyfold, nourishing the plain into Taiwan's largest granary. Hatta Yoichi's professional dedication and wholehearted spirit of service, like the ceaseless flow of the Chianan Canal's waters, has flowed into the grateful hearts of countless farmers and is remembered to this day. Because of the reservoir's special dam-building technology, its water storage capacity was the largest in East Asia at the time, drawing admiration from civil engineers worldwide; the American Society of Civil Engineers specially named Wushantou Reservoir the "Hatta Dam."

This harsh truth may disappoint readers, but it has made me realize that I am not only a creator, but even more a recorder. Perhaps some photographs will move your heart, and others will make you close the book and sit in thought; whatever feelings this book stirs, I humbly hope that readers will join me in enjoying the pleasure of flight, and find in it goals and reasons worth striving for, and will not begrudge small efforts in daily life that make this land a better place."
