notes.大稻埕，是臺北市大同區西南部的一個傳統地域名稱，因具有大片曬稻穀的空地（稻埕）而: Dadaocheng is a traditional place name for the southwestern part of Taipei's Datong District, named for the large flat area once used for drying rice (稻埕, "rice-drying yard"). In the first year of the Xianfeng era (1851), Lin Lantian, a native of Tong'an County in Quanzhou Prefecture, moved from Jilong (present-day Keelung) to Dadaocheng to escape pirate raids, and set up shop there, beginning Dadaocheng's commercial activity. In 1853, the Sanyi people and the Tong'an people fought the "Dingxia Jiao Pin" factional feud over mooring rights at Bangka wharf; the Tong'an people of Xiajiao, unable to resist, fled to Dadaocheng carrying their Xiahai City God temple's deity with them. Trade at the wharves along the Tamsui River next to Dadaocheng gradually flourished. After the opening of the Tamsui port in 1860, Dadaocheng became Taipei's most prosperous center for the distribution of goods, mainly trading in tea and cloth. Dadaocheng's tea trade, led by foreign trading houses, not only expanded in market size but also created astonishing wealth and prosperity. Entering the Japanese colonial period, Japanese merchants pushed back against the foreign trading houses' influence, shifting their main markets toward Japan and Southeast Asia instead. After the war, Dadaocheng gradually lost its function as a river port as the Tamsui River silted up, and Taiwanese tea, unable to compete with Ceylon black tea, gradually declined. Afterward, Taipei's urban area gradually developed eastward, the population moved out in large numbers, and Dadaocheng became an old, peripheral district of the city. (Wikipedia)
notes.大雁塔名稱由來。玄奘所着《大唐西域記》中記載，他在印度所聞僧人「埋雁建塔」的傳說: The origin of the name "Big Wild Goose Pagoda." In the "Great Tang Records on the Western Regions" (大唐西域記) written by Xuanzang, he recorded a legend he heard from monks in India about "burying a wild goose and building a pagoda," which explains the origin of the name of Xi'an's Big Wild Goose Pagoda. According to the legend, at a monastery in the kingdom of Magadha in India, the monks followed Hinayana Buddhism and were permitted to eat the "three kinds of pure meat" — namely goose meat, deer meat, and calf meat. One day, a monk saw a flock of geese flying overhead and said, "Today we have nothing to eat — surely the Bodhisattva knows our hunger!" As soon as he finished speaking, a goose fell dead in front of him. Startled and delighted, he told all the monks in the monastery, and they all believed that the Buddha was teaching them through this. So, at the spot where the goose had fallen, they buried the goose and built a pagoda, calling it the Wild Goose Pagoda. During Xuanzang's travels to study and obtain Buddhist scriptures in India (from 629 to 645 AD, during the Tang Dynasty's Zhenguan era), he visited and paid homage to this Wild Goose Pagoda. After returning home, while lecturing on the scriptures at Ci'en Temple in Chang'an, in order to store the scriptures, Buddha statues, and relics he had brought back from India, he built a brick pagoda in 652 in the western courtyard of Ci'en Temple, modeled on the style of the Indian Wild Goose Pagoda, and named it the Wild Goose Pagoda. The character "Big" (大) was added before the name to signify Mahayana Buddhism.

pref.克羅埃西亞的普萊特維斯湖泊國家公園，由黒河和白河匯合，引出16座連續跌落，藍綠晶: Croatia's Plitvice Lakes National Park is formed by the confluence of the Black River and the White River, giving rise to sixteen lakes cascading one into the next, their waters a crystalline blue-green. Woven among them are more than ninety waterfalls of varying size and height and differing form—some plunging in a wild, hanging torrent, others tangled and webbed like netting. As the flowing water strikes the limestone shelves and the glittering, translucent surface of the lakes, it scatters into dancing spray and curling mist. The moss, algae, and grasses along the shore, together with the lush firs, white pines, and beeches encircling the lakes, and the drifting white clouds above, set off the resplendent color of the lake and its light. Walking the boardwalk, drifting by boat upon the lake, watching the flying falls, listening to the sound of the water……
pref.初春四月，遊日本本州能登半島，一日午后，乘坐火車自和倉溫泉北上穴水，參訪來迎寺。: In early spring, in April, traveling the Noto Peninsula of Honshu, Japan, one afternoon I took a train north from Wakura Onsen to Anamizu, to visit Raikō-ji Temple. The streets of the small town of Anamizu were quiet, with a few schoolchildren scattered on their way home, and a Takkyubin delivery truck passing by. Though the plum blossoms had already opened, the cherry trees had only just stirred from their spring slumber, their branches plain and bare, save for an occasional cherry branch swaying in the wind.

pref.從紐西蘭南島的 Christchurch，北上 Aoraki / Mt. Coo: From Christchurch on New Zealand's South Island, we drove several hundred kilometers north to Aoraki / Mt. Cook National Park. The journey was long, the road winding past rolling hills and sloping meadows so green they seemed ready to drip. White sheep, now scattered, now gathered in flocks, stood out vividly against the reflected blue sky. Farther on, distant mountains kept pace alongside us, lakes dotted the landscape, clouds drifted light and unhurried, and stands of trees swayed in the wind. At dusk we arrived at the Hermitage Inn within the park. In the vast, hazy twilight, I looked about at the dim silhouettes of the mountains and saw only a crescent moon hanging alone in the heavens; a chill rose on every side, and in that clear solitude, with no one else in sight, I could not help feeling the same desolate wonder as in the old lines: "Beneath the pines I asked the boy; he said his master had gone to gather herbs, only somewhere on this mountain, hidden too deep in cloud to know where."
